body:
**Starts** once #75 is merged.

**Status, 2026-10-22:** steps 1 to 3 are done, in #91. Steps 4 to 7, the replays, are done, in a second PR, which closes this issue.

## Design

- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/code-review.md), sections 3, 4.2, 4.4, and 4.5.
- [Review rubric](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/review-rubric.md): the bar the fixer reads.
- `src/code-review/post-findings.ts`: posts a `review.json`'s findings on a PR, the way the "Code review" workflow does. It takes the PR and commit from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, `PR_NUMBER`, `HEAD_SHA`, and `GH_TOKEN`.
- `.claude/skills/fix-pr/SKILL.md`: the fixer.
- `src/code-review/fix-input.ts`, `check-fix.ts`, and `post-fix.ts`: print the fixer's input, check its answer, and post it as the fixer's app. Each script's first lines say how to run it.
- `src/code-review/app-token.ts`: makes a token for the reviewer's or the fixer's app (#92).
- #91's decisions comment: the decisions made while writing the skill and the code.

## Open questions

- ~~Does the fixer read the decisions comment? It's doing the implementer's job, so the implementer's reasons may help it, unlike the reviewer. (Moved from #71.)~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: yes. The reasons keep it from undoing a decision, such as renaming a tool back. Write it into code review design 4.5.
- ~~Does the fixer see the notes? Code review design section 3.2 has it fix a note on lines it's already changing, but section 4.2 gives it only the findings marked "fix". It can't fix a note it never sees. One way is to hand it the notes on the files it changes. Raised 2026-10-20 in chat, while finishing #75's labeling.~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: the fixer acts only on findings marked "fix", and never fixes a note, even on lines it's changing. Each extra change gives the next review new lines, and "lines it's already changing" is too loose for an agent to apply the same way twice. Notes stay on the PR for Joe. Write it into code review design 3.2 and 4.2.
- ~~How does a test run give the fixer a round's findings?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: through a draft PR, so the fixer reads them exactly as the reviewer posts them today, and the same prompt works in the test and in CI. Opening or pushing to a draft doesn't start a review (DEVELOPMENT.md section 7).
- ~~Does each replay draft get the original PR's decisions comment? Step 4 copies only the description, so the fixer would have no decisions to read.~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: yes, copy it onto the draft.
- ~~What does the fixer do in a replay when it would edit or open an issue? It may only push and comment there.~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: it writes what it would put in the issue into its reply. The subagent prompt says so.
- ~~What does "set aside" mean?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: only work planned for later, in an open issue. A finding the fixer won't fix is "not fixed": below the bar, or wrong. One Joe has to decide on "needs attention", such as a fix that would undo a decision, change a config file, or set aside a security hole. The "Set aside" list in the PR description is dropped. Written into code review design 3.6 and 4.4.
- ~~Where do the fixer's replies go?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: on each finding's own thread, starting with a marker for the outcome. A finding in a review body gets a conversation comment of its own. The reviewer gets the findings from code, without the replies (#93). Written into code review design 3.6 and 4.3.
- ~~How does Joe keep track of what's set aside and what needs attention?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: code keeps one summary comment, updated after each fix round, with links to each finding and its reply. Code resolves the threads that are fixed or not fixed. Joe resolves the rest, or ticks a checkbox for a finding in a review body. Written into code review design 4.4.
- ~~Who writes on the PR, the fixer or code?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: code. The fixer returns JSON with an outcome per finding, which code checks and then posts. In a run by hand, the fixer runs the same check on its answer. Each agent gets its own GitHub App (#92). Written into code review design 4.5.
- ~~In a replay, what does the fixer give as the issue for a finding it would set aside in a new issue? It can't open one there, so there's no number, and the check refuses `set_aside` without an open issue. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat.~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: the fixer never opens an issue, so there's always a number. See the next question.
- ~~When does the fixer set a finding aside?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat: it's called "deferred" in the fix loop, to keep it apart from CLAUDE.md's "set aside". A finding is deferred only when it holds up and is above the bar, an open issue already plans work on the same code that the fix fits better, and nothing breaks in normal use while it waits. The work goes in that issue's open questions. When no issue fits, the fixer fixes it, or it needs attention when it's too big for the PR. Written into code review design 3.8 and the skill's step 5.

- ~~Which decisions go on each replay draft? #90's decisions are spread over four conversation comments, and some came after round 1's review ran. `fix-input.ts` reads only the first. One way: copy onto each draft only the decisions that existed when that round's review ran, merged into one comment. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat. For round 1, it doesn't come up: its review ran from 16:04 to 16:07 on 2026-10-21, and only the first decisions comment existed then, so #102 got only that one. Round 2's review started at 18:32:03, nine seconds before the second comment.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: each draft gets the decisions made before the commit its review saw, merged into one comment. #102 got the first comment. #104 got the first two, since the second's decisions were made before `3c9b58a`, though it was posted nine seconds after round 2's review started.
- ~~Does a round's draft carry the earlier rounds' findings and replies? Each round has its own draft, so round 2's draft has none of round 1's. Then the replays never test the fixer reading earlier replies, or a reply asking for a fix. #44 has Joe's "Replies to the review of 8d3d3a1" that could be posted. One way: leave it out of the replays, and test it on the first live run in #77. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat. The posting side was checked by hand on #96, over two rounds on one draft.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: left out of the replays. #77's first live run checks that the fixer reads the earlier rounds' replies.
- ~~How is each run's cost measured? "Done when" asks for turns, time, and cost. A subagent's result gives tokens, tool calls, and time, but not dollars. One way: run the fixer with `claude -p --output-format json` in the worktree, which reports cost, turns, and time, and is closer to how CI will run it. That changes "Joe runs the fixer as a subagent" below. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fixer runs with `claude -p --output-format json`, in a fresh config folder, so it has none of Joe's CLAUDE.md, memories, or settings.
- ~~How does the fixer find the skill and the scripts in an old commit's worktree? The skill's commands use paths like `npx tsx src/code-review/fix-input.ts`, which aren't in the old commits. The prompt has to give `main`'s copies by full path, and fill in the PR number for `$ARGUMENTS`. Running `npx tsx <full path>/src/code-review/fix-input.ts <n>` from inside the worktree works: gh takes the repo from the worktree, and git the checked-out commit. Checked on #96. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the run script copies this branch's skill into the fixer's own config folder, with `main`'s full paths for the scripts and the rubric. It's saved as `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/run-fixer.sh`, on Joe's machine.
- ~~How does a replay keep the fixer from deferring to work planned after the round? The fixer searches today's open issues, not the ones open when the round ran. On #98, #44 round 2's replay, it deferred the F6 to #55. #55 was opened a day after that review, and its item was written after the hand fix, since it says to take out the hand fix's `touchedBy()`. One way: the replay's system prompt gives the round's date, and says to defer only to an issue opened before it. That doesn't catch an older issue edited later. Raised 2026-10-22 in chat.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: it doesn't need to. A replay is a basis for watching the fixer's behavior, not a copy of how the round went, so it works from today's issues.

## Do

Joe runs the fixer by hand, with `claude -p` on his machine, to see how it works and tune its prompt. It gets tested on two PRs' rounds:

- **PR #44,** the trip server. Its findings came from the stock review, and were labeled with the rubric in #75. Rounds 1 to 3 had findings above the bar. Round 4 had none, so the fixer doesn't run on it.
- **PR #90,** weather data. Its findings came from our reviewer, as it posts them today. Round 1's one check (V1), rain vs snow, was checked and counts as an F3, the way Joe relabels a check (code review design 4.2). Round 2 had one F6. Round 3 had only a note, so the fixer doesn't run on it.

1. **Write the decisions above into code review design 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and 4.8.** Done when the docs say the fixer reads the decisions comment, acts only on findings marked "fix", fixes no notes, and returns JSON that code checks and posts on each finding's thread, and that code keeps the summary.
2. **Write the fixer as the `fix-pr` skill, in `.claude/skills/fix-pr/SKILL.md`,** as code review design 4.5 describes. It reads the review rubric, and what code prints: the PR description, the decisions comment, the findings marked "fix", and the earlier rounds' replies. It checks each finding first (3.5), and a fix comes with a test (3.4). It writes what it defers into issues' open questions, runs `npm run check`, makes one commit, and returns a reply for each finding as JSON (3.6). Done when the skill is written and the review skill's layout is followed where it fits.
3. **Write the code around the fixer,** in `src/code-review/`: what prints its input, the check of its answer, and what posts the replies, resolves the threads, and updates the summary (code review design 3.6, 4.4, and 4.5). Done when its tests pass, and the posting is checked by hand on a replay's draft.
4. **Build each round's inputs.** Each round is replayed from the commit its review saw, not from the fixer's last result. Then each round is tested on its own, and it lines up with what was done by hand. Done when there's a `review.json` for each of these rounds, in the format `src/code-review/review-result.schema.ts` checks:

   | Round | Commit the review saw | Fixed by hand in | Findings from |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | #44 round 1 | `8d3d3a1` | `9a68517` | `scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/items/44r1.json` |
   | #44 round 2 | `9a68517` | `3035d77` | `.../items/44r2.json` |
   | #44 round 3 | `3035d77` | `ae79839` | `.../items/44r3.json` |
   | #90 round 1 | `829efb1` | `3c9b58a` | Run 39631417046's `review-transcript-1` artifact |
   | #90 round 2 | `3c9b58a` | `67338a4` | Run 39653578216's `review-transcript-1` artifact |

   - #44's base is `8fe14f4`. Its items have only the claim and the place, so give each one the label the labeling rounds settled on, from the last round that labeled it (`scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/`, on Joe's machine). Write a `labelReason` for each.
   - #90's artifacts are deleted after 30 days, on about 2026-11-20. Download them first. In round 1, change the V1's label to F3.
   - #90's two `review.json` files are saved in `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/`, on Joe's machine, as `90r1-review.json` and `90r2-review.json`. They're as the reviewer returned them, so round 1's V1 still needs changing to F3.
   - #90's base is `5a00613`, where it branched from `main`.
5. **Replay each round, and compare.** For each round, push a branch at the round's base commit and one at the reviewed commit, named `replay/<pr>-base` and `replay/<pr>-round-<n>`. Open a draft PR from one to the other, with the original PR's description, and copy its decisions comment onto it. Post the round's findings on it with `post-findings.ts`, as the reviewer app (#92). Run the fixer as a subagent in a worktree of that branch. It commits in the worktree, and doesn't write to GitHub. Where it would write into an issue, its reply says what it would write. Then post its answer with the fixer app's token (#92). The skill, the rubric, and the fixer's code in `src/code-review/` aren't in the old commits, so point the subagent at this branch's copies. Run `npm ci` in each worktree, since the packages differ by commit. Done when each round has the fixer's commit and reply on its draft, next to the hand fix.

   How it went on #96, the hand check of step 3, run from the repo root unless it says the worktree:

   ```sh
   git push origin <base>:refs/heads/replay/<pr>-base <reviewed commit>:refs/heads/replay/<pr>-round-<n>
   gh pr create --draft --base replay/<pr>-base --head replay/<pr>-round-<n> ...
   # Post the findings as the reviewer. HEAD_SHA is the reviewed commit's full SHA.
   eval "$(npx tsx --env-file=.env src/code-review/app-token.ts reviewer)"
   GITHUB_REPOSITORY=nimbusscale/road-trip-agent PR_NUMBER=<draft> HEAD_SHA=<sha> \
     npx tsx src/code-review/post-findings.ts <review.json> <not-posted.md>
   git worktree add <dir> replay/<pr>-round-<n>
   # In the worktree, after the fixer answers:
   eval "$(cd <repo> && npx tsx --env-file=.env src/code-review/app-token.ts fixer)"
   npx tsx <repo>/src/code-review/post-fix.ts <draft> <answer.json>
   ```
6. **Tune the prompt, and replay again** where the fixer went wrong. Done when Joe agrees the results are good enough to try on a live PR.
7. **Close the draft PRs, and delete the replay branches.**

## Done when

- For each round in the table, the replays' PR shows the fixer's result next to what was done by hand: each finding, what the fixer did with it, and its turns, time, and cost.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

Two PRs. #91 did steps 1 to 3. A second PR does steps 4 to 7, and closes this issue. The first live run, by hand on a new PR's review, is the first item in #77.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

Split from #71.
title: A fix agent for review findings

body:
**Starts** once #76 and #92 are merged, and #93's PR is merged. All three are merged: #93's PR, #109, merged 2026-10-22, so build from `main`.

## Why

The fix loop lets an agent fix the CI review's findings before Joe reads a PR. Each push to a PR gets a review. When the review marks findings "fix", the fixer fixes them and pushes, and the push starts the next review. That goes on for up to three fix rounds (code review design 4). So Joe reads code that's already been reviewed and fixed, and the loop shows how two agents work together through a PR. #76 built the fixer and tried it by hand. This issue runs it in CI.

## Design

- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/code-review.md), sections 4.6 and 4.7.

## Open questions

- ~~Are cleanups, the findings about reuse, speed, or style that are notes at best (code review design 4.1), saved up for a separate pass now and then, so they're fixed without feeding the next review? (Moved from #71.)~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: no. Nothing is built for it. When Joe wants a cleanup pass, he runs `/simplify` by hand on a branch.
- ~~How can the workflow tell that a review ran, when all its commands were blocked?~~ (Moved from #71, then from #75 on 2026-10-20.) The loop stops on a review that marks nothing "fix", so a review whose commands were all blocked would end the loop and get the "ready for Joe" label. One way: the `claude -p` JSON output lists `permission_denials`, and the workflow could fail the step when it isn't empty. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: two checks. The reviewer's answer takes the fixer's shape: `status` ("done" or "stopped"), `reason`, always a sentence, and `findings`, empty when stopped. The `review-pr` skill tells it to stop when it can't do a step it needs, such as reading the description, the list of earlier findings, or the diff. The review step fails on "stopped", and shows the reason in the job summary. As a backstop, the step also fails when the answer is "done" with no findings and `permission_denials` isn't empty. None of the last six reviews would have tripped that by mistake.
- ~~How do the fix loop and the reviewer keep track of V1 findings, the ones marked "check"? V1 means the label depends on a fact the reviewer can't check from the repo (review rubric, V1). Joe suggested listing them in the PR description, but DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 keeps that to the task and the "Done when" results. Set aside on 2026-10-20 until the loop runs, to see how the signals between the agents work in practice. (Moved from #75 on 2026-10-20.)~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: by hand. A check's thread stays open. Joe has the fact checked, replies on the thread with a marker from his account, and resolves it. The summary doesn't list checks. Written into code review design 4.2. Revisit if checks get lost among the notes.
- ~~Code review design section 4.8 records each finding's outcome from the first PR our reviewer reviews. That's #83, before the loop exists. Until the loop runs, who records the outcomes, and where: a row per review in section 5, or a file per PR? Raised 2026-10-20 while opening #83.~~ Dropped 2026-10-22 in chat. Each finding's outcome is in its thread's marker, so nothing is written down by hand. The round write-ups moved from code review design section 5 to `research/code-review/review-rounds.md`, which isn't added to anymore. Code review design 4.8 and 4.9 say so.
- ~~Should the review wait for the tests to pass? The "Code review" and "Check and deploy" workflows run in parallel, so a PR with failing tests still gets reviewed, at about $0.75 a run, on code that has to change anyway. In the loop, the fixer would also spend a round on findings while the tests fail. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat, while reviewing #83.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: no change. The pre-commit hook runs `npm run check`, tests included, and the fixer runs it before it commits, so a failing test rarely reaches a review. Accepted for this project.
- ~~How does the fix job know the fixer stopped early?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat, in #76: the fixer returns JSON, checked with `--json-schema`, and a stop is `"status": "stopped"` with its reason (code review design 4.5).
- ~~How does `claude -p --json-schema` check the fixer's answer? The answer schema is a choice between two shapes, "done" and "stopped". The API refuses that: "input_schema does not support oneOf, allOf, or anyOf at the top level". Without a top-level `"type": "object"`, it refuses it for that instead.~~ One way: make the answer one object, with `status` and the other fields nullable, and let `check-fix.ts` check which fields go with which status. Found 2026-10-22 in #76, while setting up the first replay. A replay runs the fixer by hand on a draft copy of an old PR's review round (#76, step 5). Checked with Claude Code 2.1.308. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: one flat object, with three keys that are always filled in. `status` is "done" or "stopped". `reason` is always a sentence: why it stopped, or for "done", a summary of the round, which the job prints. `replies` is always a list, and empty when stopped. `commit` is dropped, since code reads the checked-out commit from git, and pushes it when it's a new commit on the PR's head. Each reply's `issue` is renamed `deferredTo`, so it's clear it's the issue a deferred finding goes to. It stays `null` for the other outcomes. `check-fix.ts` checks what the schema can't: a "done" answer has at least one reply, and a "stopped" one has none.
- ~~How does the fix job keep the sandbox's empty files out of the fixer's commit? When the sandbox runs, it makes empty files in the checkout for paths it protects that don't exist yet: `.npmrc`, `.gitmodules`, `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `bunfig.toml`, `.yarnrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, and six `.env.*` files. `.gitignore` covers none of them, so a fixer that runs `git add -A` would commit them.~~ One way: have the job fail when the fixer's commit adds an empty file, or have the skill name the files it stages. Found 2026-10-22 in #76's first replay, with Claude Code 2.1.308. `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1` turns the sandbox on by itself in that version, even with no sandbox settings. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: add the 13 paths to `.gitignore`. Then `git add -A` skips them, `check-fix.ts`'s check for uncommitted changes doesn't see them, and local sandboxed runs don't show them either. The project uses only npm, and versions are locked, so the list holds.
- ~~How does the fix job keep the fixer from editing the config files in DEVELOPMENT.md section 6?~~ Locally, `.claude/settings.json` has ask rules for them. In CI, Claude Code ignores that file (`.github/workflows/code-review.yml` says why), so the rules don't apply. One way: pass deny rules for those files in the job's `--settings`. Edit rules don't cover a shell command such as `sed`, so the job could also fail when the fixer's commit touches one of them. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat, while reviewing #91. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: before the fixer starts, the job turns the "ask" rules in `.claude/settings.json` into deny rules, and passes them with `--settings`, along with the sandbox settings. The sandbox mounts each denied file read-only for the fixer's commands, so `sed` and `echo >>` fail too, not only the Edit tool. Tested with Claude Code 2.1.308. Two things the job has to do, found in the test: drop each rule's leading `/`, since in an inline `--settings` string it matches nothing, and expand a wildcard in a file name, such as `tsconfig*.json`, into the exact files, since the sandbox skips those rules. A folder rule, such as `.claude/hooks/**`, works as it is. New disable comments can't be blocked by a file rule, since they go in ordinary code files. So `eslint.config.js` bans them: turn on `@eslint-community/eslint-comments/no-use`, and set `ban-ts-comment`'s `"ts-expect-error"` to `true`. Joe approved that config change 2026-10-22 in chat. There are none in `src/` or `web/` today.
- ~~What starts the fixer after Joe replies "fix it" on a finding that needs attention?~~ Code review design 4.5 says the next fixer acts on the reply, and `fix-input.ts` passes it on. But 4.6 starts a run only on a push, and runs the fix job only when the review marks a finding "fix". A reply isn't a push. A push by Joe gets a review that won't post that finding again, so the fix job is skipped. One way: run the fix job when the review marks a finding "fix", or when a finding that needs attention has a new reply from Joe. Deferred 2026-10-22 from #91's third review ([finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/91#discussion_r4349315316)). Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fix job runs when the review marks a finding "fix", or when a finding that needs attention has a reply from Joe after the fixer's. The review job outputs both counts. Joe starts the run by re-running the PR's latest "Code review" run, from the Actions tab or with `gh run rerun <run-id>`. No new trigger. To leave such a finding alone, Joe resolves its thread instead of replying. The cap of three fix rounds still holds.

- ~~How does the fixer edit a skill file, such as `.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md`? With Claude Code 2.1.308, `claude -p` refuses an Edit tool write under `.claude/` unless the permission mode is `bypassPermissions`. An allow rule such as `Edit(.claude/skills/**)`, or `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, doesn't help. Tested 2026-10-22 on #93's PR, #109, where round 1's fixer answered "needs attention" for that reason. Skill files aren't config files (DEVELOPMENT.md section 6), so a fix in one is in the fixer's scope.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fixer doesn't get to edit skill files. A finding whose fix is in one needs attention, and Joe or Claude Code fixes it by hand, as on #109's round 1. Bypassing permissions was turned down, since it would also drop the `--allowedTools` list. Write this into code review design 3.6's list of what needs attention.
- ~~The `fix-pr` skill runs `npx tsx src/code-review/fix-input.ts` and `check-fix.ts`. `npx tsx` fails in Claude Code's sandbox, since the tsx command opens a socket that the sandbox refuses (`listen EPERM`). `node --import tsx <file>` works. Found 2026-10-22 by the first review of #109, which fixed the reviewer's skill.~~ One way: change the `fix-pr` skill the same way, before the fix job runs it in the sandbox. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat, and done in PR #111: the `fix-pr` skill runs both scripts with `node --import tsx`, and code review design 4.5 says so. `npx vitest` works in the sandbox, checked the same day.
- ~~ESLint lints `scratch/`, where the `fix-pr` skill tells the fixer to put throwaway files. On #109, round 1's fixer left `scratch/block-listen.cjs`, and `npm run check` then failed on it. Each CI run starts from a fresh checkout, so this only bites when the fixer leaves a `.js` or `.cjs` file there and then runs the check in the same run.~~ One way: have the skill say to delete its throwaway files before `npm run check`, or ignore `scratch/` in ESLint, which is a config change. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: ESLint ignores `scratch/`. Joe approved the config change, and it's made in its own small PR before #77 starts.

- ~~On #109, after the cap, Joe also took `Bash(npx tsx:*)` off the reviewer's allowed tools, since `npx tsx` fails in the sandbox. The fix job's `--allowedTools` list starts from the replays' list, which has it too (see "Do").~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fix job's `--allowedTools` leaves `Bash(npx tsx:*)` out, as code review design 4.5 says (PR #111).
- ~~A "Fixed" marker tells every later review to check the fix again, with no end. Example: round 1 posts finding A, and the fixer replies "Fixed". Round 2 posts finding B, that A's fix didn't work, and B gets "Not fixed: wrong". In round 3, the list from `review-input.ts` still tells the reviewer to check A's fix and post it again if the problem is still there, and to leave B alone. So the reviewer could post the same problem a third time. Deferred 2026-10-22 from #109's sixth review ([finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/109#discussion_r4352696590)). Joe left it unfixed, since it needs a disputed fix and then a "wrong" on the dispute.~~ One way, if it shows up in the loop: a line in the `review-pr` skill's step 6 saying that when two earlier findings make the same point, the later one's instruction wins. Accepted 2026-10-22 in chat: nothing is built for it now. If the loop shows it happening, add that line to the `review-pr` skill's step 6.

## Do

- **First, the fixer runs by hand on a real PR.** That's done in #93, on its own PR, for up to three rounds (#93, "Do" step 4). Agreed in chat on 2026-10-21, and moved to #93 on 2026-10-22. #76's replays ran one round per draft, so #93's rounds are the first test of the fixer reading earlier rounds' replies on one PR. Done on #109: three fix rounds, and six reviews in all. `research/code-review/review-rounds.md` records each one, under "PR #109". The runner was `scratch/code-review-eval/fix-loop-93/run-round.sh` on Joe's machine, and each round's transcript and answer are saved beside it. Write up what it did in this issue's PR. Joe doesn't need to look before the job is built. Still untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix. That needs Joe, so leave it for him, and say so in the PR.
- **Make the changes the settled open questions above say,** as code review design 4.5 to 4.7 now describe them (written in by PR #108): the fixer's answer shape, the deny rules for the config files, the reviewer's `status` and the backstop check, and when the fix job runs. Check the sandbox's placeholder files in CI, with the fix job's Claude Code version, against the list in `.gitignore`.
- Give the fix job the fixer app's token, from #92.
- Start the fix job's `--allowedTools` from the list #76's replays used, in `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/run-fixer.sh` on Joe's machine. It has `rm`, which the reviewer's list doesn't, since `claude -p` refuses any command that isn't on the list. Found 2026-10-22 in #76's first replay, where the fixer deleted a file with `git clean -f` instead. Leave out `Bash(npx tsx:*)` (open questions above).
- Turn off Claude Code's attribution in the fix job's `--settings`: `"attribution": {"commit": "", "pr": "", "sessionUrl": false}`, as on Joe's machine. Claude Code adds a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line to commits by default, and no commit or PR in the project carries one. Found 2026-10-22 in #76's first replay.
- Add the fix job, the cap of three fix rounds, and the "ready for Joe" label to the "Code review" workflow.
- Run the loop on real PRs.

## Done when

- A PR goes through the loop and gets the "ready for Joe" label, and its runs' transcripts are saved.

## Ends in

A PR, left for Joe's review. Don't merge it. The loop runs on this PR itself, which is the "Done when" check. If the review still marks a finding "fix" after three fix rounds, stop and wait for Joe.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

title: The fix loop in CI

body:
## Design

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 4 ("Errors are readable").
- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 4 ("A broken rule throws `RuleError`").

## Open questions

- What kinds of errors do tools return, and does the agent need to tell them apart? `RuleError` covers both broken rules, such as "A trip is at most 14 days long," and bad formats, such as "A date is written YYYY-MM-DD." Every readable error reaches the agent the same way: "Nothing was changed." and then the message, with no kind. If the coordinator's instructions describe errors as broken rules, it may spend tokens working out which rule a format error broke.
- Should broken stored data come back as a readable error? A stored date that isn't real, such as "2027-02-30," throws `RuleError` when the trip loads. Write tools load inside `writeReplyOrReadableError` (`src/tools/tool-reply.ts`), so the agent reads "Nothing was changed. 2027-2-30 isn't a real date." and may think its own input was wrong. Broken stored data is a bug, so a failed call may fit better. Raised by review finding 31-9 in the code review labeling for #75.
- Where are the error kinds written down, so builders and the coordinator's instructions agree? No design doc names `RuleError`. Only DEVELOPMENT.md section 4 and the code do.

## Do

- Decide the error kinds, which ones come back to the agent as a readable message, and what the agent is told about each. Write them into tool design section 4.
- Change the code to match.
- Say what the coordinator's instructions need to cover about errors, for #48 and #65.

## Done when

- Tool design section 4 lists each error kind, and whether the agent reads it or the call fails.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

title: How errors reach the agent

body:
A research spike: can Claude Code's sandbox limit the network for the fix loop's agents in CI? The answer decides whether our reviewer can run `node`.

## Design

- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/code-review-rubric-v2/design/code-review.md), section 4.1 (our reviewer can run node, to test a claim) and section 4.6 (neither the reviewer nor the fixer gets WebFetch or WebSearch). Both are added in #81.
- `.github/workflows/code-review.yml`, the "Review the PR" step. Its comments explain the token scrub, the sandbox tools it installs, and why node is blocked today.

## Open questions

- ~~Does `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB` turn on the sandbox's network limits, or only the scrub?~~ Settled 2026-10-20 in chat: only the scrub. With the scrub alone, node and curl reached example.com and pypi.org, and git reached gitlab.com ([run](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39473872334)).
- ~~How are allowed domains set for a `claude -p` run in CI, since Claude Code ignores the allow rules in `.claude/settings.json` there?~~ Settled 2026-10-20 in chat: with `--settings`, which CI applies even though the workspace isn't trusted. The settings are in code review design section 4.6 (#81).
- ~~Can the sandbox let `git` and `gh` reach GitHub, and refuse every other site?~~ Settled 2026-10-20 in chat: yes. `git ls-remote` and `gh api` worked. Other sites were refused with "host is not on the allow list", and so was a command that tried to go around the proxy ([run](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39474232216)). Plain `node` fetch reaches nothing, GitHub included. `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` wasn't tested, and the docs are taken as the answer.
- ~~Which domains do the reviewer and the fixer need? At least `github.com` and `api.github.com`. The fixer's `npm run check` may need none, if the packages are installed before it starts.~~ Settled 2026-10-20 in chat: `github.com` and `api.github.com`. `npm run check` passed inside the sandbox with no network. Only `gh api` was tested, so another `gh` command that needs more domains gets them when it comes up.
- ~~Does the fixer push from inside the sandbox, or does the workflow push after the fixer finishes?~~ Settled 2026-10-20 in chat: either works. A push from inside the sandbox reaches GitHub. Sandboxed commands can read the checkout's token, which Joe accepts, since the fixer's token is a GitHub App token limited to this repo (code review design section 4.6).

## Do

- Answer the open questions. A test run in CI is fine, such as one where a command tries `node -e "fetch('https://example.com')"`.

## Done when

- Joe agrees the open questions are answered.

## Ends in

A decision: whether the reviewer runs `node`, and how the agents' network is limited. **Decided 2026-10-20 in chat:** the reviewer runs `node` to test claims that need no outside access, and each agent's commands run in Claude Code's sandbox with only GitHub reachable. A claim that only an outside service can settle gets V1. Written into code review design sections 4.1 and 4.6 (#81, 6203c93).

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

---

The code review research is spread across `research/`, and the labeler prompt that tested the rubric in #75 is only on Joe's machine, in `scratch/`, which is gitignored. Later work needs that prompt, such as the checker in #86. An agent working from its own clone can't see `scratch/`. One folder for the code review research also makes it easier to find.

## Design

## Open questions

- Should the labeling rounds' summaries go in too, such as round 4's `summary.md`? They're the evidence for the rubric changes in #81. Joe has them in `scratch/code-review-eval/labeling/`, and would hand them over.

  - `research/code-review-evaluation.md`

The folder held a clone cut at the reviewed commit, the rubric (section 3.1 only), a `task.md` naming the PR, its base commit, and its task, and an `items.json`. Each item had only an ID, the claim, and the file and line. The labeler got no earlier labels or reasons. Its tools were read-only, plus `git`, `jq`, and `node`, with no `gh` and no web tools. It answered with a JSON array, one object per item: `{"id", "label", "reasoning", "checked"}`, where `checked` lists the files and lines it read. Two labelers labeled the same items, each on its own, and a script compared them by group.
  - Its paragraph about `plan/development-plan.md` was only for the old corpus, which came from before work was tracked in GitHub issues. Keep it in the copy, marked that way.

## Done when

A PR.

body:
## Why

Issues are now written for Joe, and for Claude Code sessions that have chat history or memory. They often lean on that context: terms agreed only in chat, files only on Joe's machine, or decisions described as "as discussed". Joe may later run headless agents that pick up an issue when it moves to a status, and build it with only the repo and the issue. So an issue has to make sense to an agent with neither chat nor memory.

Example: the first draft of the checker issue (#86) pointed to files in `scratch/`, which is gitignored, and used terms defined only in chat, such as "act" for the group of findings that need something done.

## Design

- DEVELOPMENT.md section 9, which says how issues are tracked and what sections an issue body has.

## Open questions

- ~~Should the issue sections in DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 get a "Why" section, as #86 has? Today they're Design, Open questions, Do, Done when, Ends in, and Settled in.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: yes. Why is the first section, and DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 lists it (PR #103).

## Do

The work has two parts, done in this order.

**1. Write the rule.** In a PR:

- Add a rule to DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 that an issue must stand on its own:
  - It says why the work matters.
  - It defines any term that isn't defined in a design doc.
  - It points only to things in the repo or on GitHub, never to chat, memory, or files on Joe's machine.
  - It says what's been decided, and where.
- Give the rule a short test: could a new Claude Code session, with only the repo and the issue, build it the way it's meant?

**2. Bring the Backlog in line.** Once the PR is merged:

- List the issues in the project's Backlog status with the command in DEVELOPMENT.md section 9.
- Check each one against the rule and the test. Rewrite the body of any that fails. Keep its meaning, and don't make new decisions while rewriting it.
- If a rewrite needs an answer that isn't written down anywhere in the repo or on GitHub, add it to that issue's open questions instead of guessing.

## Done when

- DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 has the rule and the test.
- Every issue in the Backlog meets the rule.

## Ends in

A PR for part 1. Part 2 is edits to issue bodies on GitHub, made after the PR is merged.

**Settled in:** the PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment, and Joe agrees by approving the PR.

title: Write issues so they stand on their own

body:
**Starts** once #84 is merged.

## Why

Our CI reviewer, the `review-pr` skill (#75, #83), finds problems in a PR and labels each one with the rubric in code review design section 3.1. The label puts each finding in one of three groups:

- **Act:** fix (F1 to F7) and check (V1). Something has to happen.
- **Note:** N1 to N6 and NF2 to NF5. Posted for Joe to read. Nothing is fixed.
- **Drop:** D1 to D3. Not posted. Listed in `not-posted.md`.

The group is what matters. The label is the rule that picked the group. The reviewer labels its own findings, so it may not be objective about them. The worst case is a true finding dropped as D1, which only `not-posted.md` shows.

This issue builds a checker, so we can tell how often the reviewer puts a finding in the wrong group. We run it by hand, not in CI. If findings land in the wrong group too often, we add a checker to the CI review, as its own agent. The checker is also how later prompt or model changes get compared on the same reviews, so the reviews from #83 on become a corpus (code review design section 4.9).

## How the rubric was tested before

In #75, the rubric was tested by labeling old findings four times. Each time, two labelers labeled the same findings, each in a fresh context, and a script compared them. `research/code-review/labeler-prompt.md` (#84) has the prompt and how it was run. The point to keep: a labeler gets each finding's claim and location, but never an earlier label or the reason for it.

## Design

- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/code-review.md):
  - Section 3.1, the rubric.
  - Section 4.2, the kinds of findings and `not-posted.md`.
  - Sections 4.8 and 4.9, testing the reviewer, and the corpus.
- `research/code-review/labeler-prompt.md`, from #84.
- `.github/workflows/code-review.yml`. Each review run uploads an artifact named `review-transcript-<attempt>`, kept for 30 days. It holds:
  - `review.json`, the `claude -p` output. Its `structured_output.findings` has every finding, with `file`, `line`, `label`, `finding`, and `labelReason`.
  - `not-posted.md`.
  - The transcript, under `.claude/projects/`.

## Open questions

- **Where are review runs kept past 30 days?** Options are a local folder, a Spaces bucket, or something else. The choice should carry over to other projects. #83's first runs expire around 2026-11-19.
- **Can the labeler use `gh issue view` to check D3?** On the new PRs, D3 means a code comment hands the work to a GitHub issue, so the labeler has to read that issue's body. The old labelers had no `gh`. One way is to allow only `gh issue view <n> --json number,title,state,body`, as the reviewer does.
- **The reviewer read the PR description and the earlier inline comments as they were at review time.** Both can change later. Does the checker take them from the transcript, or does each review run need to save them?
- **What counts as "too often"?** That is, how many findings in the wrong group before a checker joins CI.
- **Is it a skill, a script, or both?**
- **Should it count findings that flip between a D label and another group from one round to the next?** The next review doesn't see the D labels (code review design section 4.2), so each round labels a dropped finding again on its own. A flip is a labeling disagreement found without running the labelers. Comparing each round's `not-posted.md` with the posted comments would find them.

## Do

- Decide where review runs are kept, and keep them from #83's runs on.
- Build the checker:
  - It takes one review run's findings, and gives the labelers only each finding's ID, its claim (the `finding` text), and its file and line. They get no label and no `labelReason`.
  - Two labelers run as `research/code-review/labeler-prompt.md` describes.
  - A script compares them with each other, and with the reviewer, by group. It lists every finding where any of the three disagree, for Joe.
- Run it on #83's reviews and the PRs after it.
- Write the checker, the groups, and where runs are kept into code review design sections 4.8 and 4.9.

## Done when

- For each finding in the reviews it ran on, the result shows the reviewer's group and the two labelers' groups, and lists every disagreement.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

title: A checker that relabels the reviewer's findings, run by hand

body:
## Why

The reviewer, the `review-pr` skill in `.claude/skills/review-pr/`, is told in its step 4 to read `DEVELOPMENT.md` and `design/README.md` in full, and then only the design docs the PR touches. On #83, its last run read only the diffs of those two files, since the PR changed both. If it skips them on a PR that writes app code, it reviews without the coding rules. That would show up as missed findings, not as an error.

`design/code-review.md` was also split on #83: the rubric moved to `design/review-rubric.md`, so the reviewer reads the rubric without the real past reviews in `code-review.md`. That only works if the reviewer doesn't open `code-review.md` anyway. On a PR that doesn't touch the review code, it has no reason to.

## Design

- Code review design section 4.1, what the reviewer does.
- Code review design section 2: each "Code review" run saves its transcript as the artifact `review-transcript-<attempt>`, for 30 days.

## Open questions

- None yet.

## Do

- For each PR that our reviewer reviews, and that doesn't change the review code, download the run's artifact with `gh run download <run-id>`.
- In the transcript, the `.jsonl` file under `.claude/projects/`, list the files the reviewer read. Count both the Read tool and Bash commands such as `cat`. Note for each PR:
  - whether it read `DEVELOPMENT.md` in full,
  - whether it read `design/README.md` in full,
  - whether it opened `design/code-review.md`.
- If it skips a file it should read, or opens `code-review.md`, propose a change to the skill in a comment here.

## Done when

- Joe says he's comfortable with how the reviewer works. There's no set number of PRs. (Changed 2026-10-21 from 3 PRs.)
- Each PR checked has a comment here with its results, and the last one either says no change is needed or proposes one.

## Ends in

A decision, or a PR if the skill changes.

**Settled in:** chat.

It returned no findings. The run took 8 turns, 29 seconds, and $0.27 at API prices.

**Whether no findings was right.** Yes, for this PR. The change is small, and the rule does what #72 asks. The gaps I can see are below the bar, such as a dynamic `import("zod")` not being caught, which nothing uses.

**What it means for the skill.** Skipping most of `DEVELOPMENT.md` probably made no difference on this PR, but it could on a bigger one. No skill change proposed yet. Checking each PR from here on.

## PR 2: #90 (run 39631417046)

- **`DEVELOPMENT.md` in full:** no. It didn't open it at all, though the PR adds app code in `src/`.
- **`design/README.md` in full:** yes. It ran `cat design/README.md`.
- **Opened `design/code-review.md`:** no.

**What it did read and run.** It read the rubric in full, the PR description, the earlier findings, and the diff. It left out the saved responses, which kept the diff small. It read issue #63's body, the Open-Meteo design in full, Google design section 3, tool design 2.5 and section 4, and technical spec 6.3. It grepped the source for the helpers the new code calls. It ran a short `node` script over the saved Google responses to see which precipitation types they hold, which is how it found its first finding. The run took 19 turns, 139 seconds, and $1.07 at API prices.

**Its findings.** Three, all worth having:

- **V1, rain vs snow:** real. Google sends `SNOW` and `RAIN_AND_SNOW` as the precipitation type. On 2026-10-21, Leadville, CO got "Light snow" with a 40% `SNOW` chance, which the tool would have called "40% chance of rain". The reviewer couldn't reach Google to check, so V1 was the right label. Checked, it's an F3.
- **NF2, a window that runs into the future:** real, and the label fits. Open-Meteo refuses an end date after today with HTTP 400. It only happens for a late-December stay planned in the first week of January.
- **N6, a stale sentence in Google design section 3:** real, and the label fits.

It missed nothing I know of. Skipping `DEVELOPMENT.md` didn't visibly cost a finding on this PR.

**Proposed skill change.** `DEVELOPMENT.md` has now been skipped on both PRs: section 4 only on #88, and not at all here. Step 4 says to read it, but by step 4 the reviewer is already following the diff into the design docs. Both runs began by reading the rubric in full, in step 1. So I propose moving the read into step 1: "Read `design/review-rubric.md`, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and `design/README.md` in full, in one command." Step 4 would then cover only the design docs the PR touches. This would be a small PR that changes the review code, so that PR's own review wouldn't be checked here.

## PR 2, second run: #90 (run 39653578216)

This run reviewed the push that renamed the tool and fixed the first run's findings.

- **`DEVELOPMENT.md` in full:** no. It didn't open it at all, the same as the first run.
- **`design/README.md` in full:** yes. It ran `cat design/README.md | head -60`, and the file is 17 lines.
- **Opened `design/code-review.md`:** no.

**What it did read and run.** It read the rubric in full, the PR description, and the earlier inline comments and reviews. It read the diff, the new weather source files in full, the Open-Meteo design in full, tool design 2.5 and section 4, and the weather tool's tests. It ran a short `node` script over the saved Open-Meteo responses to look at the precipitation values. It took 12 turns, 109 seconds, and $0.74 at API prices.

**Its findings.** One, and it's real:

- **F6, "Days with rain" counts snow days:** Open-Meteo design 2.3 counts a day with at least 1 mm of `precipitation_sum` as a rain day. But `precipitation_sum` includes snow, as its water. So a January stay in Leadville would show a high rain share on days that only snow. The line it points to isn't in the PR's changes, so it was posted as a review comment, not inline. The label fits, since the code follows the design and the design is what's wrong.

It didn't repeat the first run's New Year finding, which is still in the code. That's right, since the lines haven't changed and the earlier inline comment already makes it. It missed nothing I know of.

**Skill change.** This adds a third run that skipped `DEVELOPMENT.md`, so the proposal above to read it in step 1 still stands.

## PR 2, third run: #90 (run 39654548978)

This run reviewed the push that counts rain days from Open-Meteo's `rain_sum`.

- **`DEVELOPMENT.md` in full:** no. It didn't open it at all, the same as both earlier runs on this PR.

It missed nothing I know of. It didn't repeat any earlier finding.

**Skill change.** All three runs on this PR skipped `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and this one skipped `design/README.md` too. Neither cost a finding I know of, but the proposal above to read both in step 1 still stands.

The skill change proposed above is on hold, settled in chat on 2026-10-21. Skipping `DEVELOPMENT.md` or `design/README.md` hasn't cost a finding on any PR so far. Raise it again only if a missed finding traces back to a file the reviewer skipped.

## PR 4, second run: #91 (run 39789908735)

This run reviewed the push that fixed the first run's F2 and F6.

## PR 4, third run: #91 (run 39792221142)

This run reviewed the push that fixed the second run's F2, and changed CLAUDE.md's line to "Read DEVELOPMENT.md before writing, changing, or reviewing code." Joe asked for the change, to see whether the reviewer then reads it.

- **`design/README.md` in full:** yes, in the same command.

The read came before it looked at the CLAUDE.md diff, but CLAUDE.md is in its context from the start, and the commit list names the change. So this run can't tell the new wording apart from the reviewer seeing the change in the PR. The next PR that doesn't touch CLAUDE.md will.

It took 34 turns, 224 seconds, and $1.47 at API prices.

**Its findings.** One, and it's real:

- **F6, nothing in the workflow runs the fixer after Joe's "fix it" reply** (`design/code-review.md:207`): section 4.5 says the next fixer acts on it, but section 4.6 starts a run only on a push, and runs the fix job only when the review marks a finding "fix". A reply isn't a push, and a push by Joe gets a review that won't post that finding again.

**#107, run 39818420569.** This PR changes the review code (`src/code-review/`, the fixer's skill, the rubric, and code review design), so it's outside this issue's "Do". It's noted here because of the first two points.

- **`DEVELOPMENT.md`:** not read. The skill's step 4 says to read it.
- **`design/README.md`:** not read. Step 4 says to read it too.
- **`design/code-review.md`:** opened with a `grep` for the fixer's answer file, and its diff was read, since the PR changes it.

body:
## Why

DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 says an issue moves to Done when its PR is merged and deployed. Today nothing checks the deploy. The project's built-in "Item closed" rule moves an issue to Done as soon as the PR merges and closes it. On #88, #72 showed Done while the "Check and deploy" run was still going. If that deploy had failed, the board would have said the work was live when it wasn't.

## Design

- Systems design section 7: deploys, run by `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` on each merge to `main`.
- DEVELOPMENT.md section 9: the statuses, and who moves an item.

## Open questions

1. The workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can't change a project owned by a user account. It needs a classic personal access token with the `project` scope, stored as a repo secret. Is a new secret OK here, or is there a better way?
2. Should an issue whose deploy fails stay in In review, or go back to In progress?

## Do

- Add a step, or a job after `deploy` in `deploy.yml`, that runs only when the deploy passes. It finds the issues the merged PR closed, and moves each one's project item to Done.
- Turn off the project's built-in "Item closed" rule, so it doesn't move the item to Done before the deploy finishes.
- Update DEVELOPMENT.md section 9 and systems design section 7 to say the deploy workflow moves the item to Done.

## Done when

- After a PR that closes an issue is merged, the issue stays in In review until the deploy job passes, then moves to Done without anyone moving it.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment (DEVELOPMENT.md section 7), and Joe agrees by approving the PR.

body:
**Starts** once #76 and #92 are merged.

## Why

Once the fixer replies on each finding's thread (#76), the reviewer must not read those replies, since they hold the fixer's reasons and would color its review. Today the reviewer reads the threads itself, with `gh api .../pulls/<number>/comments`, which returns the replies too. Instead, code hands it the list of earlier findings. Agreed 2026-10-21 in chat, while working on #76.

## Design

- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/code-review.md), sections 3.6 and 4.3. Section 3.6 says how the fixer replies on each finding's thread, and the marker that starts each reply.
- `.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md`, step 2: where the reviewer reads the earlier findings today.
- `src/code-review/fix-round.ts`, from #76: reads the findings, their replies, and each reply's marker from the PR's threads.

## Open questions

- ~~Does the reviewer run the code itself, as a command in its skill, or does the workflow run it and put the list in the prompt? A command would keep `/review-pr <number>` working locally.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the skill runs it as a command, `npx tsx src/code-review/review-input.ts <number>`, the way the fixer runs `fix-input.ts`. The script reads the threads in its own process and prints only the list, so the transcript never shows a reply.
- ~~Should the reviewer's `gh api` be narrowed, so it can't read the comments on its own? Today it's allowed any `gh api` call.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: take `gh api` off the reviewer's allowed list. Step 2's two comment reads were its only use, since #75. Also lower the review job's `pull-requests` permission to `read`, so the token the reviewer holds can't post. The posting step posts with the reviewer app's token instead. `node` could still reach the API, and `gh pr view --comments` still matches the allowed prefix. The prompt forbids both, and the transcript check catches them.
- ~~When Joe or Claude Code handles a finding by hand, how does the next review learn the outcome? DEVELOPMENT.md section 7's rule against thread replies goes, and code reads a marker only from the fixer's app.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: reply on the finding's thread from Joe's own account, starting with the marker, in the UI or with Joe's `gh` login. The list takes a marker from the fixer's app or from `nimbusscale`, and ignores anyone else's, since the repo is public. The reviewer still sees only what the marker means, never the reply. Posting as the fixer's app was turned down, since it would need the app's key by hand and blur who replied.

## Do

1. **Build the reviewer's list of earlier findings,** in `src/code-review/review-input.ts`, with the code #76 adds to read the threads and their markers. It reads a marker from the fixer's app or from `nimbusscale`, and no one else. Each finding gives its text, its place, and only what the marker means for the review:
   - **Fixed:** check whether the fix worked, and post it again if it didn't.
   - **Deferred:** drop it. The list gives the issue number, since that's scope.
   - **Not fixed, or needs attention:** drop it. The list doesn't say which, or why.
   - **No reply yet,** such as a note: as today, don't post it again unless its lines changed and the problem is still there.
2. **Change the `review-pr` skill to read that list,** in place of its `gh api` calls for the comments and reviews. Change the "Code review" workflow to match: take `gh api` off the reviewer's allowed list, lower the job's `pull-requests` permission to `read`, and have the posting step post as the reviewer app, `nimbusscale-review-pr`, with the app's token from #92 (code review design 4.6). Today it posts as `github-actions[bot]`. Moved from #92 on 2026-10-22. Take out the skill's two mentions of a "Set aside" list in the description, which #76 dropped.
3. **Write it into code review design 2 and 4.3, and DEVELOPMENT.md section 7.** Section 7 says not to reply on a finding's thread, since the next review would read the reply. That rule goes once the reviewer no longer reads the threads. In its place: a finding handled by hand gets a reply on its thread from Joe's account, starting with the marker. PR #108 already wrote the decisions in, so check that the code matches them, and fix the docs where the code shows they're wrong.
4. **Run the fixer by hand on this PR, as the fix loop will.** This is #77's first step too. After each CI review that marks a finding "fix", run the `fix-pr` skill as a subagent, then post its answer with `post-fix.ts`, as the fixer's app (`app-token.ts fixer`, code review design 4.6). #76's replays did the same, with `scratch/code-review-eval/replays/run-fixer.sh` on Joe's machine. The fixer's push starts the next review. Do up to three fix rounds. Record each round in code review design section 5. Check which files each review read, and add it to #87.

## Done when

- A review of a PR whose threads have fixer replies reads the list, and its transcript shows it read no reply.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR. It has to merge before #77's first live run, where the fixer first replies on a real PR's threads.

Joe agreed 2026-10-22 in chat that Claude Code works on it while he's away:

- **Merge it** when the last review marks nothing "fix", and nothing needs Joe. Notes don't block the merge. They stay on the PR for Joe.
- **Don't merge it, but go on to #77,** when a finding needs attention, a V1 "check" finding comes up, or there's a security problem. Build #77 on this PR's branch.
- **Stop all work and wait for Joe** when the review still marks a finding "fix" after three fix rounds.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
title: Hand the reviewer its earlier findings without the fixer's replies

body:
## Why

In the fix loop, each review after the first should mostly check the last round's fixes. When review 2 or 3 finds a problem in code that review 1 already read, review 1 missed it. Then the loop finds bugs a few at a time, one round each. The cap of three fix rounds (code review design 4.6) works only if the first review finds most of what there is to find. If it doesn't, the loop stops at the cap with bugs still in the code, and raising the cap only spends more rounds on the same problem.

This issue tracks how often that happens, so we can tell whether the first review's recall needs work. Recall here means the share of the PR's real findings that the first review finds.

## Design

- Code review design 4.6: the cap of three fix rounds.
- Code review design 4.8: how the reviewer is judged.
- `research/code-review/review-rounds.md`: the write-ups of PR #39's, #44's, and #109's rounds, where the examples below come from. It isn't added to anymore.

## Open questions

This issue also collects ideas, so they aren't lost. It may turn out there's no problem worth acting on. Nothing below is settled.

- If the first review's recall turns out to be low, what's the fix? Ideas so far:
  - **Run two reviews on round 1, and merge their findings.** Each run reads and notices different things, so two runs may find more than one. It spends more where a miss costs the most.
  - **Narrow the reviews after round 1 to the last round's fixes.** Code review design 4.3 has each review read the whole PR, since on PR #44 round 2 found a bug in code round 1 had read. Narrowing would stop the PR's scope from growing each round: a fix brings new code into the diff, the next review finds something in it, and so on. PR #39's seven rounds were that. But narrowing is only safe when round 1's recall is good, since later rounds would no longer catch what round 1 missed. Joe recalls that a published review loop narrows its reviews after the third. Not checked.
- Does a smaller scope give better recall, since there's less to look at? Untested. One way to test it: on the same round, run a review of only the fixes and a review of the whole PR, and compare what each finds.

## Do

- For each PR the loop runs on, look at each finding marked "fix" or "check" in review 2 or later. Note whether review 1 could have found it: its lines were in review 1's diff, and no fix since changed them. A finding about a fix's own lines, or about work done after review 1, doesn't count.
- For each one review 1 could have found, note where it was:
  - **on a line the PR changed,**
  - **elsewhere in a function the PR changed,** or
  - **elsewhere,** such as another function in the file, or another file.

  The first two are what the `review-pr` skill's angle A tells the reviewer to read, so a miss there is the worse kind. A miss elsewhere is easier to understand, since only angle C, callers and callees, reaches there.
- Write the count for each PR in a comment on this issue.
- So far:
  - **PR #109:** two of four. Review 3's F2, that a "Fixed" marker from Joe still asked the fixer for a fix, was in `isAskable()`, a function the first commit changed. Code review design 3.6 already said Joe replies with a marker. Review 6's F6, that a "Fixed" marker makes every later review check the fix again, was on lines of `review-input-text.ts`, a new file in the first commit. It's a rule that goes wrong across several rounds, not a bug in one line. Both are the worse kind. Review 2's F1 and review 4's V1 were about work done after review 1. `research/code-review/review-rounds.md` has the rounds.
  - **PR #44,** before the loop: two of round 2's five findings were in code round 1 had read (`research/code-review/review-rounds.md`). Where they were isn't sorted yet.
- After a few PRs, say in a comment here whether the first review misses enough to act on, and propose what to change.

## Done when

- Joe decides whether the first review's recall is good enough, or agrees on a change to raise it.

## Ends in

A decision, or a PR if the reviewer changes.

**Settled in:** chat.

---

Raised 2026-10-22 in chat, after PR #109's four review rounds.

body:
## Why

The review step in the "Code review" workflow fails when the reviewer answers "done" with no findings, but `claude -p` refused one of its commands (code review design 4.7). That's a backstop, so a review that was stuck doesn't look clean and end the fix loop. On PR #113, the second review tripped it as a false alarm (run 39855660869, at e7e6eed). The reviewer had read the description, its earlier findings, and the diff, and it said why it found nothing. Its one refused command started with a shell variable assignment, `deny=$(node --import tsx ...); jq ...`, which matches no rule on its allowed list. On 2026-10-22, Joe chose to keep the backstop as it is, and revisit it if it fails a review that ran again.

## Design

- Code review design section 4.7, a check that the review ran.
- Code review design section 2: each run saves its transcript as the artifact `review-transcript-<attempt>`, for 30 days.

## Open questions

- None yet.

## Do

- When a review step fails on the backstop, download the run's artifact with `gh run download <run-id>`. Check in the transcript whether the reviewer read the PR description, the list from `review-input.ts`, and the diff.
- If it read all three, it's a false alarm. Add a comment here with the run, and the refused command.
- When false alarms happen again, propose a change to Joe. For example, the `review-pr` skill could say not to start a command with a variable assignment.

## Done when

- Joe decides whether the backstop or the skill changes.

A decision, or a PR if the backstop or the skill changes.

body:
## Why

An MCP server can send the model instructions of its own, as well as its tools. That exists for servers that anyone can plug into a client they don't control. We write every server and every agent, so we don't need it. Today the `trip` and `memory` servers send instructions (tool design, section 4). So the rules the coordinator follows would be split between its system prompt and two servers' instructions.

This issue moves those rules out of the servers. A rule that covers several tools goes in the system prompt of each agent that has those tools. Then everything the model is told, apart from each tool's own name, description, and input schema, is in one system prompt per agent. A system prompt is also per agent, and a server isn't. The `trip` server holds both the coordinator's tools and the workers' tools, so a rule written for the coordinator could reach a worker. It's done before #48, so #48 builds the coordinator without changing the tool servers.

## Design

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 4.

## Open questions

- ~~Does the started-trip sentence in the `memory` server's instructions move to the coordinator's prompt? The sentence is "Once the trip has started, its trip memory can't change, and user memory still can." The `trip` server doesn't state its own started-trip rule, and the rule matters only in a turn still running at midnight, when the error already says the trip has started. "User memory still can" could also lead a coordinator whose trip memory add was refused to save the note to user memory instead, which would carry a one-trip note to every later trip.~~ Settled in chat on 2026-10-23: drop the sentence. The model learns the rule from the error, as with the `trip` server. Tool design section 4 and technical spec 3.1 still describe the rule. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-23, while reviewing PR #116.

## Do

- Change the "rule that covers several tools" bullet in tool design section 4. A rule that covers several tools goes in the system prompt of each agent that has those tools, not in an MCP server's instructions, and not in each tool's description. When the rule applies to more than one agent, its text is written once in code, and each agent's prompt that needs it includes it. A tool's description holds only what's specific to that tool, and the system prompt never repeats it. When an agent evaluation shows a model missing one of these rules, the rule is repeated in the description of the tool where it was missed. Drop the sentence about where Claude Code puts server instructions.
- Remove `instructions` from the `trip` server (`src/tools/trip-server.ts`) and the `memory` server (`src/tools/memory-server.ts`), along with the constants that hold the text, and fix any test or comment that refers to them. Fix the comment on `createWeatherServer` too, which says it needs no instructions because it has one tool.
- Don't put the removed text anywhere in this issue. #48's "Do" list holds it, word for word, and puts it in the coordinator's instructions. The started-trip sentence is dropped (open questions).

## Done when

- No MCP server in `src/` sets `instructions`.
- Tool design section 4 says where a rule that covers several tools goes, as above.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
title: Move the MCP server instructions into the agents' system prompts

body:
**Starts** once #48 is merged.

## Why

On every turn, the model reads its system prompt and each tool's name, description, and input schema as one unit. That text is spread over several files, and some of it exists in no file in the form the model gets it:

- Tool descriptions and input schemas are in separate files, such as `src/tools/memory-tools.ts` and `src/tools/memory-input.schema.ts`.
- Some numbers are filled in from `settings.json`, such as "at most 300 characters." The coordinator's system prompt from #48 fills in numbers the same way.
- The input schemas are written in Zod, and the model gets the JSON Schema that Zod makes from them. That step can add things the source doesn't show. Example: Zod gave every whole-number input a maximum of 9,007,199,254,740,991, which the model would read as a real limit.

So comparing two versions of what an agent is told, such as before and after a change an evaluation (#53) tests, means reading diffs in several files and working out the final text by hand. This issue writes what each agent sees into one checked-in file per agent. A PR's diff of that file is the change to what the model sees, with the numbers filled in and the JSON Schema as the model gets it.

## Design

- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), sections 2 and 5.

## Open questions

None yet.

## Do

- Add a test that builds what each agent sees, and compares it to that agent's checked-in file, such as `coordinator.view.md`. The coordinator is the only agent so far. The file has the agent's system prompt, built with the real `settings.json`, then each of its tools: name, description, and input JSON Schema. Get the tools through an MCP client, as the `trip` and `memory` server tests already do, so the file shows them as the SDK gets them. Use Vitest's file snapshot (`toMatchFileSnapshot`), so a file that doesn't match fails the test and prints the lines that differ. A normal test run never writes the file.
- Add `npm run agent-views`, which rewrites the files. It runs only this test with Vitest's `-u`, so it never updates any other snapshot. The check stays in `npm run test`, so `npm run check` and CI fail on a stale file.
- Write both into DEVELOPMENT.md: the command in section 2, and in section 5, that a change to anything an agent reads, or to a setting it shows, comes with its rewritten view file in the same commit. Each issue that adds an agent adds its file to the test.

## Done when

- `coordinator.view.md` is checked in and shows the coordinator's system prompt and every tool it has, with numbers filled in from `settings.json`.
- Changing one tool description, without running `npm run agent-views`, makes `npm run check` fail with the changed line. Running it fixes the failure. Put the failure output in the PR.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
title: A checked-in file of what each agent sees

body:
## Why

This is a learning project, and the point is to see how the agent works. The browser chat (#52) shows only the user's messages and the coordinator's replies, plus "Working: update_trip_brief…" while a tool runs. Everything in between is hidden: what the model thought, which tools it called with what input, what each tool sent back, and how long the turn took. The terminal chat shows some of it, but Joe wants to use the browser. This issue adds a raw view to the browser chat that shows the whole loop of each turn.

## Design

- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), section 4.
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 10.1.

Decided when the issue was written, and in the struck-out open questions below:

- **The chat is a list of cards, like other chat apps.** The user's messages are cards on the right. The coordinator's replies are cards on the left.
- **A "Raw" toggle on the chat view adds more cards on the left.** Off, the chat shows only the user's messages and the coordinator's replies. On, the left side also shows the cards listed under Do: the turn's start, the message the model got, thinking, tool calls, tool replies, other system messages, and the turn's end, in the order they happened. The right side doesn't change. There's no second column.
- **The raw cards aren't saved.** They live in the browser tab's memory only. A reload, or opening a session again, shows the conversation with no raw cards. The transcript is not changed.
- **The tab keeps the raw cards whether the toggle is on or off.** So turning it on partway through a session shows them for the turns already sent from this tab.
- **The coordinator's thinking is shown as a summary.** The coordinator already thinks: adaptive thinking is the Agent SDK's default for its model. But the thinking text comes back empty. The saved transcripts hold thinking blocks with only a signature, the encrypted form the API needs to go on with the conversation. The SDK's `thinking: { type: "adaptive", display: "summarized" }` returns a summary of the thinking in those blocks. It changes only what's returned, not how much the model thinks or what it costs.

## Open questions

- ~~What each item in the details column looks like: readable cards like the terminal chat, or each Agent SDK message as raw JSON?~~ Settled 2026-10-23 in chat: readable cards, laid out as above. Thinking in italics, a tool call as its name and input, a tool reply in a box. Long tool inputs and replies are cut to about 15 lines, with a "show all" to open the rest.
- ~~Who sees the toggle: every user, or only Joe?~~ Settled 2026-10-23 in chat: every user. The cards hold only the user's own trip data, plus the model's name and the tool names.

## Do

- Turn on summarized thinking in the coordinator's options (`src/agent/coordinator.ts`), and add a line about it to the technical spec.
- Pass these to the browser, in order, for each turn the tab sends (`src/agent/turn-event.ts`, `src/api/turn-stream.ts`). Each becomes a raw card on the left:
  - The turn's start: the model and the tools it was given.
  - The message the model got, with the app's lines added, such as the date and the resumed line (technical spec 5.2). It goes on the left, since the app wrote those lines, not the user.
  - Each thinking summary, reply text, tool call with its full input, and tool reply with its full text and whether it was an error.
  - Any other system message from the SDK, such as a retry, as its subtype and data.
  - The turn's end: how long it took, the number of model calls, input and output tokens, and why it failed, if it did.
- Show the conversation as cards, and add the "Raw" toggle and the raw cards to the chat view (`web/src/chat-page.tsx`, `web/src/chat-state.ts`).

## Done when

- A test with a fake turn (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5) shows each kind of item above reaching the browser's stream.
- On the deployed site after the merge (systems design, section 7), Joe turns on "Raw", sends a message that makes the coordinator call a tool, and sees on the left, in order: the start, the message with the app's lines, a thinking summary, the tool call with its input, the tool's reply, the reply text, and the end with its time and tokens.
- With "Raw" off, only the user's messages show on the right and the coordinator's replies on the left.
- After a reload, the conversation is restored as cards, with no raw cards.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
