body:
**Starts** once #54 is merged.

## Why

The coordinator can't read the whole itinerary of a long trip. #54 built `read_itinerary`, and measured a whole read of a 14-day trip at about 38,000 tokens. Claude Code returns at most 25,000 tokens of a tool result, so the tool refuses the read with an error. Technical spec 5.2 has the coordinator read the whole itinerary at the start of each session, after a resume, and to answer "what's left to decide?". On a trip longer than about a week, it gets the error in all three. This spike finds out how to handle that: read less in those cases, put less in a whole read, or allow a larger reply.

## Design

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1 (`read_itinerary`, its size limit, and the measurement).
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), sections 5.2 (when the coordinator reads the whole itinerary) and 7.2 (what the coordinator sees).

## What #54 found

**The trip measured.** A 14-day loop from Las Vegas with 8 stays, five stops a day, three candidates for each stop and stay, and a second set of three for about one in four of them. That's 312 candidates. It's `src/domain/fourteen-day-example.fake.ts`. Its places are made up, but each has the length of a real Google name, type, and address. Tool design 2.1 had estimated a trip like this at about 300 candidates and 20,000 tokens.

**The size of its whole read.** 72,264 characters, in 683 lines. The API counts it as 38,271 tokens for `claude-opus-5-5`, the coordinator's model. That's 1.89 characters a token. Plain English, the first 20,000 characters of DEVELOPMENT.md, came to 2.9. Tokens were counted by sending the text through the Agent SDK and taking the input tokens less those of a one-word prompt, since the plan token has no API key for the token count endpoint.

**Where the tokens go.** Measured on an earlier version of the read, at 75,613 characters:

- The 312 candidate lines were 44,832 characters and 23,183 tokens, about 60% of the read. Each gives its set, name, place ID, short line, and visit and detour times. The selected one also gives its rationale.
- Everything else was 30,800 characters and 16,177 tokens: stays, days, legs, schedules, stop lines, and check results.
- The read holds 496 IDs, such as `place_k7m2x9qa`. IDs and short lines are what make the read cost more tokens than prose.

**Scoped reads.** Each day of the trip reads at 5,202 characters at most. A stay read gives every candidate's full details, so a 3-night stay is 28,104 characters, and a 1-night stay about 12,000. A stay of 5 nights or more at this density would be refused too.

**What the tool does now.** It refuses any reply over 40,000 characters, about 21,000 tokens at 1.89, with "Can't read the itinerary: it's too large to return. Read one day, stay, or stop at a time instead." At this density, a whole read fits a trip of about a week.

**What Claude Code does over the limit.** It saves a tool result over 25,000 tokens to a file, and gives the model only the file's path and a short preview. The coordinator has no Read tool, so for it the result is cut off, with nothing to say so. 25,000 is Claude Code's default for MCP tools, and nothing in Claude Code 2.1.301, which SDK 0.3.301 ships, treats in-process servers differently.

**Every read stays in context.** A 38,000-token read at the start of each session uses that much of every later turn's input, and goes out of date with the next change.

## A realistic whole read

[Research doc: making a whole itinerary read smaller](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md) (`research/itinerary-read-size.md`) measures a realistic 14-day read, what each change to the format would save, and what each costs the coordinator. Today's whole read of a busy trip is 66,260 characters and 34,498 tokens. The proposal in its section 5 brings it to 27,582 characters and 15,291 tokens. `research/itinerary-read-size/slim-read-proposed.txt` shows the proposed format, on the same trip with its last stay still undecided.

## Open questions

- ~~In each of the three cases in technical spec 5.2, what does the coordinator need from the read? Example: "what's left to decide?" needs empty and proposed stops and lodging, and open warnings, not every candidate.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: the start of a session needs the open warnings, the forecast notes, and the trip as it stands. A resume needs the same, and also has to spot what the conversation never heard about (#147 asks whether to add a list of changes). "What's left to decide?" needs the empty and proposed items, the open warnings, and the approvals. None needs every candidate. Research doc section 2.1.
- ~~Can a whole read carry less, and still do its job? Example: each stop's selected place and a count of its other candidates, leaving the full list to a read of the stay or stop. Tool design 2.1 says a whole read gives every candidate, so this would change it.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: yes. The whole read gives each picked place with its town, counts the other candidates by set, and leaves out the rationale, weather text, and tier rules, which the itinerary view shows. Research doc section 5.
- ~~Should there be a new scope for a summary, such as one for what's left to decide?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. The slimmer whole read is about 15,000 tokens on a busy 14-day trip, and answers "what's left to decide?" itself.
- ~~Could the coordinator read a long trip a stay at a time in those cases, with only instructions changing?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. It would lose the parts that only a whole read shows, and the slimmer whole read fits.
- ~~Should the limit go up? Claude Code has a setting for it, `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`. Check whether it applies to an in-process server through the Agent SDK, and what a larger read costs in context on every later turn. Tool design 2.1 now says raising the limit isn't the fix, so a yes changes it.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. The slimmer whole read fits under 25,000 tokens, and under the tool's 40,000-character limit, so neither changes. Research doc section 10.
- ~~Can the format itself cost fewer tokens, such as fewer IDs, without making a read harder for the coordinator to act on?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: yes, in the ways research doc section 5 lists. Fewer IDs, no: the coordinator needs each one to act on its item (section 13).
- ~~Whichever way is chosen has to reach the parts that only a whole read shows today, raised in PR #128's review (finding comment-4364853766). The check results whose subject is the itinerary, such as the trip length ("The trip is 10 days, and the brief asks for 11."), are in no day, stay, or stop read, since each of those filters results by subject (`checkLines` in `src/tools/itinerary-lines.ts`). Nor are the start and end places, the dates, or the rejected places. So on a trip whose whole read is refused, the coordinator never sees them, and the start-of-session bullet on open warnings misses the trip length. A stay's lodging, lodging candidates, and weather text are only in a whole read or a read of that stay, never a day read (`dayScopeLines`). At the measured density, a stay of 5 nights or more is refused too, so for such a stay they can't be read at all. Reading a stay at a time leaves both cases open, and a slimmer whole read leaves the long stay open.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: the slimmer whole read keeps the trip-level check results, the start and end places, the dates, the rejected places, and each stay's lodging line, so they stay in reach. A stay's weather text and lodging candidates come from a read of that stay. Research doc section 5.

- ~~If a whole read gives no candidate names (version L in the research doc), how does the coordinator find which stop or stay to read when the user names a candidate in chat, such as "let's do the Desert Pearl"? For lodging, `find_place` gives the town, which points to a stay. For a meal stop, a town can hold several stops, so it would read the whole stay or try stops one at a time. A wrong guess fails quietly: `select_user_place` refuses a place that's already a candidate only on that same stop, so on another stop it adds the place as one the user named, and the stop that offered it stays undecided. The options so far: keep each undecided item's candidate names, with or without place IDs, and measure both; or a `read_itinerary` scope by place ID. Research doc section 7 says the coordinator recovers after one wasted call, since the error tells it to use `select_candidate` (tool design 2.1, `select_user_place`). That's true only when it guessed the stop or stay that offered the place.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: a new tool searches the trip's own places by name, with string similarity, and always returns the closest few with where each sits in the trip. The whole read gives counts, not names. Research doc section 6. Still open there: whether `select_user_place` should say when the place is a candidate on another stop or stay (section 6.4).

## Do

- ~~Measure what each option saves on the 14-day trip, in characters and in tokens as the API counts them.~~ Done in the research doc, in PR #140.
- ~~Propose an answer for each open question.~~ Done, and each is settled above.
- Now that PR #140 is merged, a new session writes the design changes in research doc section 11 into the design docs, in a PR. The research doc's sections 5, 6, and 9 hold the agreed details. The same session plans the build and opens its issues. It decides how to split the build, such as whether the read change and `find_in_trip` are one issue or two. Joe asked for that decision to be made there, not in the spike.

## Done when

- Joe has agreed to an approach. Done on 2026-10-26: research doc sections 5, 6, and 9.
- The approach is written into the design docs: tool design 2.1, technical spec 5.1, 5.2, and 7.2, as research doc section 11 lists.
- The issues to build it are open.

## Ends in

A decision.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
title: Spike: whole itinerary reads of long trips

body:
## Why

The agent's behavior should be checked again after any change to its instructions, its tools, or its model, by rerunning a set of evaluations (#53). Self-hosted Arize Phoenix is the chosen platform. It traces each turn, and it has datasets, experiments, and a side-by-side view of two runs. promptfoo was the earlier choice, but it's only a test runner, and Joe already knows it. Phoenix gives more, and it's new for Joe to learn, which is the point of this project. So try hard to make Phoenix work. promptfoo is the fallback, used only if nothing else works. This spike works out how Phoenix works with this app and writes it down. The build in #53 is planned later, from what the spike finds.

## Design

- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 5.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 3.1 (tests).
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 11.
- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), sections 5, 6, and 8.
- Phoenix docs: [Claude Agent SDK tracing (TypeScript)](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/typescript/claude-agent-sdk), [TypeScript client](https://www.arize.com/docs/phoenix/sdk-api-reference/typescript/arizeai-phoenix-client).

## Open questions

None yet.

## Do

Joe isn't available while this runs, so don't stop to wait for answers. When a choice comes up, make it, and list it in the PR's decisions comment. When something can't be made to work, write down what was tried and what failed, then go on to the next item.

Answer each of these with working code, and write the answers into `research/agent-evaluations.md`. Lay it out like `research/agent-sdk-tool-scoping.md`: a note that it's research, not design, then Method, then Results.

- **Run Phoenix locally** as a Docker Compose profile in `compose.yaml`, listening only on `127.0.0.1`, with no sign-in. Use an exact image version. Say where its data is kept: its own volume, or a database in our Postgres.
- **Trace a coordinator turn** on the Agent SDK version the app uses (0.3.301). Add `@arizeai/phoenix-otel` and `@arizeai/openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk`, at exact versions. The SDK must be imported through the instrumented module, or no traces are made, so `runTurnWithSdk` in `src/agent/coordinator.ts` needs to change. Say whether each MCP tool call shows up with its inputs and result, and whether token counts do.
- **Run one evaluation case from start to finish** with `@arizeai/phoenix-client`: a dataset, a task, and scorers, run as an experiment. The task sends scripted user messages to the coordinator through the same code as `npm run chat` (`src/chat.ts`), for a new trip. Use a fresh user UUID each run, so memory starts empty. Set up any memory beforehand through the memory code (persistence design section 8.8), not SQL. Use the "user or trip memory" check from #48: "we never eat at chains" goes to user memory, and "skip I-35 this time" goes to trip memory.
- **Score it two ways.** One scorer is code that reads what was saved from the database. One is a model judge on `claude-haiku-5-5`, called with the Anthropic SDK and paid for with the Max plan's API credits. Its key is in `.env` as `JUDGE_API_KEY`. The name must not start with `ANTHROPIC_`. An `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` would make the coordinator bill API credits instead of the plan (`src/agent/claude-env.ts`). Check that the coordinator still runs on the plan token. The key is short-lived. If it's missing, or a call fails because it expired, write that down and go on without the judge. If the judge can't run on the Anthropic API for another reason, write down why. Don't switch to another provider, such as OpenRouter. Joe decides that, since he'd need credits there.
- **Run the case five times.** Say how much the results change from run to run. Using the token counts in the SDK's result message for each turn, and the judge's API usage, say how much one run takes.

Push the spike code to `spike/phoenix-evals`, a branch that never gets a PR, so merging the doc doesn't delete it. The doc links to it. The code doesn't need to pass `npm run check`.

## Done when

- `research/agent-evaluations.md` answers each Do item, with the output that shows it.
- On the spike branch, one command runs the case and the experiment shows up in Phoenix.

## Ends in

A PR with the research doc.

## Settled in

The PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment, and Joe agrees by approving the PR.
title: Research spike: agent evaluations with Arize Phoenix

body:
**Starts** once #136 is merged.

## Why

Joe can't see how the coordinator worked on a turn once it's over, except in the chat's raw view, which isn't saved. Agent evaluations (#53) also need traces to build on. The #132 spike traced the coordinator in Arize Phoenix, but only on Joe's machine, from `npm run chat`. This issue runs one Phoenix on the server, and sends it the traces of every web chat turn: from the live site, and from `npm run dev` on Joe's machine. So there's one place to see both. This issue is only about traces. Evaluations stay in #53.

A **trace** is the record of one turn. It's made of **spans**: one for the turn, and under it, in order, one for each model call and one for each tool call. A Phoenix **project** holds its own traces, sessions, and token totals.

## Design

- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), sections 2 (the server and its containers), 6 (local development), and 7 (deploys).
- [research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.1 (Phoenix in Docker Compose), 2.2 (tracing a coordinator turn), and 3. The spike's code is on the [`spike/phoenix-evals`](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/tree/spike/phoenix-evals) branch.
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 10.1 (the chat view and the raw view).

## Open questions

- ~~How does Joe's machine reach the server's Phoenix?~~ Settled in chat on 2026-10-25: through an SSH tunnel, the same way it reaches the server's Postgres. Phoenix listens only on the server's `127.0.0.1:6006`, with no sign-in, so nothing new is open to the internet. Joe runs `ssh -N -L 6006:127.0.0.1:6006 root@projects.jjk3.com`. Then the local app sends traces to `http://127.0.0.1:6006`, and his browser opens the Phoenix UI at the same address. Putting Phoenix on the internet through Caddy was the other option. It would need Phoenix's sign-in, an API key for sending traces, and a second site, and every trace would be behind one login page.
- ~~How does the page show that traces aren't reaching Phoenix?~~ Settled in chat on 2026-10-25: when the page loads, the app checks that it can reach Phoenix, and the page shows a green check or a red X. It's a reminder to bring up the tunnel when running locally, or to look into Phoenix on the server before starting a session. It doesn't check that each turn's spans arrived. The chat works the same either way. Spans that can't be sent are lost, with no retry.
- ~~How are the server's traces told apart from local ones?~~ Settled in chat on 2026-10-25: two Phoenix projects. The server sends to `road-trip-agent`, and Joe's machine sends to `road-trip-agent-local`. Local traces are mostly test chats, from the local database, so they'd skew the server's session list and token totals if they were mixed. One project with a tag was the other option. It would need a filter typed in each time.
- How do the user's message and the right token counts get into each turn's trace? Phoenix's instrumentation for the Agent SDK shows the streamed prompt as `{}`, and leaves cache tokens out of its input count, so a 48,255-token turn shows as 8. The spike replaced it with spans from our own code, `TurnTrace`, which has the user's message, and each model call's thinking, tool calls, and tokens (research doc sections 2.2 and 3). The proposal is to bring `TurnTrace` over. Moved from #53 on 2026-10-25.

## Do

- **Run Phoenix on the server.** Add a `phoenix` service to `compose.yaml`, like the spike's (research doc section 2.1), with these changes:
  - It's in the `production` profile, like `backup`, so it starts only on the server. Locally, no Phoenix runs. The local app sends to the server's, through the tunnel.
  - Its port is published only on the server's `127.0.0.1:6006`. The server's app reaches it over the Compose network.
  - Its image is `arizephoenix/phoenix:20.26.0`, the spike's. Its data is a SQLite file in its own volume, `phoenix-data`, not in our Postgres, so it isn't in the nightly backup. Sign-in and Phoenix's own telemetry are off.
  - `ops/deploy.sh` doesn't change. Its image list is only for our private images, which need a sign-in to pull. Its `docker compose up` pulls Phoenix's public image on its own.
- **Trace each coordinator turn.** Bring `TurnTrace` (`src/agent/turn-trace.ts`) and its changes to `runTurnWithSdk` and `src/agent/turn-event.ts` over from the spike branch, with tests on fakes. Bring it as #136 leaves it, so a worker's spans go under the coordinator's `Agent` tool span once workers exist (#60, #61, #64). No worker exists yet, so tests use a fake worker's messages. Add the packages it needs at the spike's exact versions: `@arizeai/phoenix-otel` 2.3.0, `@opentelemetry/api` 1.9.1, and `@arizeai/openinference-semantic-conventions` 2.15.0. `@arizeai/phoenix-client` isn't needed for traces, so it stays with #53. Besides the spike's `session.id`, each turn's span gets the user's ID as `user.id`, so a trace shows whose chat it is.
- **Send the traces from the app and from `npm run chat`.** Both set up the tracer when they start, in `src/main.ts` and `src/chat.ts`, from two values in the environment: Phoenix's address and the project's name. Check them with Zod in `src/config/env.schema.ts`. `compose.yaml` sets them for the server's app container: `http://phoenix:6006` and `road-trip-agent`. So the server's `.env` doesn't change. Locally, `.env` has `http://127.0.0.1:6006` and `road-trip-agent-local`. Add both to `.env.example`. Spans are sent in batches, so flush them before the process ends.
- **Show whether Phoenix can be reached** when the page loads, with a green check or a red X, next to the line from `web/src/health-status.tsx`. Every user sees it. The app does the check, since it's what sends the traces, and on the server the browser can't reach Phoenix. When Phoenix can't be reached, nothing else changes: chat turns run as before, and the deploy's call to `/api/health` doesn't fail.
- **Write it down.** In the systems design: the new container, and how Phoenix is reached on the server and from Joe's machine, with the tunnel command. In the functional spec: the check or X on the page. In DEVELOPMENT.md section 2: bring up the tunnel before `npm run dev` or `npm run chat`, and open the Phoenix UI.
- **Merge and deploy,** then check the live site and local `npm run dev` yourself (Done when). Sign in as Claude Code's own Supabase user (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5), and send one chat turn to each through `/api`. Then check Phoenix through the tunnel, such as with its REST API. A Claude Code session can open the tunnel itself with the command above. That was checked on 2026-10-25. The green check and red X need no sign-in, since the health line shows before sign-in.

## Done when

- `npm run check` passes.
- After the deploy, with the tunnel up, a chat turn sent on `roadtrip.jjk3.com` shows up in Phoenix's `road-trip-agent` project. Its trace has the turn span, with the user's message and the reply, and the model call spans, with their thinking and tokens, and the tool spans, in order. The Sessions view groups the chat's turns.
- With the tunnel up, a chat turn sent to local `npm run dev` shows up in `road-trip-agent-local`.
- With the tunnel down, the local page shows the red X, and a chat turn still works. With it up, the page shows the green check.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment (DEVELOPMENT.md section 7), and Joe agrees by approving the PR.
title: Trace web chats in Phoenix on the server

body:
## Why

#135 brings the #132 spike's `TurnTrace` to `main`, so each coordinator turn is traced in Phoenix. `TurnTrace` only knows about the coordinator. Once workers exist (#60, #61, #64), a turn will also hold the workers' model calls and tool calls, often several workers at once (technical spec section 1). `TurnTrace` assumes every message from the SDK is the coordinator's, so it may mix a worker's model calls and tokens into the coordinator's spans. This spike finds a way to trace workers on the spike branch first, so `TurnTrace` has the right shape before it's on `main` with tests.

A **worker** is a subagent the coordinator starts with its `Agent` tool (technical spec section 6). A **trace** is the record of one turn, made of **spans**: one for the turn, and under it, in order, one for each model call and one for each tool call (research doc section 2.2).

## Design

- [research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.2 (spans from our own code) and 3 ("Workers aren't traced yet"). The code is `src/agent/turn-trace.ts` on the [`spike/phoenix-evals`](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/tree/spike/phoenix-evals) branch.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), sections 1 (the agents, and that workers run in parallel) and 6 (workers).
- The Agent SDK's types for 0.3.301, in `node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/sdk.d.ts`. Start from these: the `agents` option and `AgentDefinition`, `parent_tool_use_id` on the SDK's messages and stream events, the `forwardSubagentText` option, and `getSubagentMessages()`. By default, the SDK sends only a worker's tool calls and tool results, not its text or thinking.

## Open questions

- How are a worker's turns traced in Phoenix? The Do items below answer it. Moved from #60 on 2026-10-25, where it was raised for the stay researcher.

## Do

Joe isn't available while this runs, so don't stop to wait for answers. When a choice comes up, make it, and list it in the PR's decisions comment. When something can't be made to work, write down what was tried and what failed, then go on to the next item.

Do the work on `spike/phoenix-evals`, with Phoenix running locally as in the #132 spike (`docker compose --profile evals up -d phoenix`). The server's Phoenix comes later, in #135. The code doesn't need to pass `npm run check`. That branch never gets a PR, so its code never reaches `main`. Push the code there, and make the research doc change on its own branch off `main`, for the PR.

- **Add a throwaway worker** on the spike branch, since no real one exists yet. Pass it to the coordinator in the SDK's `agents` option, and add `Agent` to the coordinator's allowed tools. Give the worker one tool from an MCP server the app already has, such as `find_place`, and a short instruction, such as "find two coffee shops near the place you're given." Put it on a different model from the coordinator's, such as `claude-sonnet-5-5`, so its model calls are easy to tell apart. Find a message for `npm run chat` that makes the coordinator start it, and one that starts two at once. The coordinator's instructions name no worker, so it may not call one from a message alone. If it doesn't, add a line about the worker to its instructions on the spike branch.
- **Find out what the SDK sends from a worker,** with `includePartialMessages` on as `TurnTrace` has it, and with `forwardSubagentText` off and on. For each, say whether these come through, and how each is tied to the worker: its thinking, its text, its tool calls with their inputs and results, and each of its model calls' token counts. Say whether the turn's result message counts the worker's tokens in its usage. If a worker's thinking or tokens can't be had from the stream, try `getSubagentMessages()`, and say what it gives and when it can be read.
- **Make `TurnTrace` trace workers.** Each worker gets its own span under the coordinator's `Agent` tool span, with its model call spans and tool spans under that, in order. Show it working with two workers at once, with neither one's spans under the other's. Check in Phoenix that the coordinator's own model call spans hold only the coordinator's tokens, and that the trace's and the session's token totals include the workers'.
- **Write the answers into `research/agent-evaluations.md`,** as a new section under Results, with the output that shows each one, such as a span tree like section 2.2's. Change section 3's bullet "Workers aren't traced yet" to say what was found, and what `TurnTrace` needs on `main`.

## Done when

- `research/agent-evaluations.md` answers each Do item, with the output that shows it.
- On the spike branch, a chat turn that starts two workers shows up in Phoenix with each worker's spans under its own `Agent` tool span.

## Ends in

A PR with the research doc.

## Settled in

The PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment, and Joe agrees by approving the PR.
title: Spike: trace workers in Phoenix

body:
## Why

The chat's "Raw" toggle shows each step of a turn as a card (functional spec 10.1). Before Phoenix, it was the only way to see how the coordinator worked on a turn. Now every turn's trace is saved in Phoenix (systems design section 10), where it can be looked at after a reload and clicked through. So Raw is a fair amount of UI code for something Phoenix does better. This issue removes it.

Four things Raw shows aren't in the trace yet, so this issue adds them first, and nothing is lost:

- **The model and the tools the coordinator was given.** Raw's first card lists them, from the Agent SDK's `init` message. Each model call's span has its model, but nothing in the trace has the tool list.
- **The Agent SDK's other system messages, such as a retry.** Raw shows each one as a card. The trace keeps only `task_started`, which starts a worker's span. So if the Claude API failed and the SDK retried, Phoenix wouldn't show it.
- **The full reason a turn failed.** Raw shows the text `failureOf()` builds in `src/agent/turn-event.ts`, such as `error_during_execution: <the SDK's errors>`. The turn span's error status has only the subtype, such as `error_during_execution`.
- **The error when the SDK throws.** Raw shows `String(error)`, from the `ended` event that `#run` in `src/agent/coordinator-turns.ts` adds when the turn throws. The trace says only "The turn ended with no result."

Two things are given up, on purpose. Phoenix gets spans in batches every few seconds, so a turn's steps can't be watched live as they stream. And users other than Joe see only the chat, with no steps. They don't need them.

A **span event** is a named, timed note on a span, with its own attributes. Phoenix shows a span's events with the span. An attribute holds only plain values, such as a string or a list of strings. The OpenTelemetry SDK drops a nested object without saying so.

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 10.1 (the chat view and the raw view).
- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), sections 4 (the browser and the app) and 10 (traces).
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.4 (thinking).

## Open questions

None yet.

## Do

- **Add to the trace what only Raw shows,** on the `coordinator.turn` span in `src/agent/turn-trace.ts`, with tests on fakes. Add the fake SDK messages the tests need to `src/agent/fake-sdk-messages.schema.ts`, such as `init`, `api_retry`, and a failed result.
  - A span event named `started`, from the SDK's `init` message, with the attributes `model` and `tools`.
  - A span event for each of the coordinator's other system messages, at the time it arrived, named by its subtype. Its fields go in one attribute, `data`, as JSON, since some fields are nested objects, such as `api_retry`'s `error`. Leave out the fields every system message has, as `turnEventsOf()` does with `SYSTEM_MESSAGE_IDS` in `src/agent/turn-event.ts`. Export that set to share it. `thinking_tokens` gets no event, as it gets no turn event today. `task_started` gets no event either, since the worker's span it starts already shows it.
  - In the turn span's error status, the text `failureOf()` builds, in place of the bare subtype. Export `failureOf()` to share it.
  - When the SDK throws, `String(error)` as the turn span's error status, in place of "The turn ended with no result." Catch it in `runTurnWithSdk` in `src/agent/coordinator.ts`, record it on the trace, and throw it again, so `#run` still ends the turn as it does today.
- **Remove the raw view from the page:** the "Raw" toggle in `web/src/chat-page.tsx`, `web/src/raw-card.tsx`, the raw cards and `shownCards()`'s raw case in `web/src/chat-state.ts`, their CSS in `web/src/app.css`, and their tests. Replies always show formatted. The line that names the tool the coordinator is waiting on stays.
- **Send the browser only the events it uses.** Keep `session`, `text`, `toolCall`, and `ended`. Remove `started`, `message`, `thinking`, `toolReply`, and `system` from `chatEventSchemas` in `src/shared/session.schema.ts`, and from `chatEventOf()` in `src/api/turn-stream.ts`. Trim `toolCall` to the tool's name, and `ended` to `failure`. Update the tests that check the old events: `src/api/chat-turns.test.ts` and `src/shared/chat-event-parser.test.ts`.
- **Remove the `message` turn event.** Only the browser used it. `#run` in `src/agent/coordinator-turns.ts` adds it after `started`, and `npm run chat` skips it. Remove it from `TurnEvent`, and remove the code and comment in `#run` that add it. The other turn events don't change, since `npm run chat` prints them.
- **Keep the thinking summary.** The coordinator's `thinking: { display: "summarized" }` stays, since the trace shows the summaries. Change the comment on it in `src/agent/coordinator.ts`, and technical spec 5.4, to say it's for the trace.
- **Fix the comments that mention the raw view or the removed events,** such as in `src/api/turn-stream.ts`, `src/shared/session.schema.ts`, `src/agent/coordinator-turns.ts`, and the header of `src/agent/turn-event.ts`.
- **Write it down.**
  - Functional spec 10.1: remove the "Raw" bullet. The trace bullet after it says each turn's steps are "also" saved as a trace, so reword it to stand on its own.
  - Systems design section 4: say the stream sends the reply's parts, the tool being called, and the turn's end. Remove the raw view from the Markdown paragraph.
  - Systems design section 10: add the `started` event, the system message events, and the failure text to the `coordinator.turn` row. Remove each mention of the raw view, in the opening paragraph and in the tokens bullet ("as the raw view's does").
- **Check it locally,** with the SSH tunnel to Phoenix up (DEVELOPMENT.md section 2). Sign in as Claude Code's own user (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5), and send a chat turn that calls a tool to `npm run dev` through `/api`. Read the stream and check that only the four events arrive. Wait a few seconds for the spans to be sent. Then check the turn's trace in Phoenix's `road-trip-agent-local` project, such as with its REST API. Joe checks the page itself in the PR review, since a session has no browser.

## Done when

- `npm run check` passes.
- Locally, a chat turn sent through `/api` streams only `session`, `text`, `toolCall`, and `ended` events.
- That turn's trace in `road-trip-agent-local` has the `started` span event on the turn span, with the model and the tools.
- Tests on fakes show a retry message from the SDK as a span event on the turn span, a failed turn's span with the full failure text, and a turn that throws with the error's text.
- In the PR review, Joe sees no "Raw" toggle, a reply that shows formatted, and the line naming the tool being called while the tool runs.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment (DEVELOPMENT.md section 7), and Joe agrees by approving the PR.

body:
**Starts** once #141 is merged.

## Why

Joe tests the coordinator by hand as it's built. Rating a turn, or a whole chat, with a note, right when it happens, records what went well and what went wrong while it's fresh. Later, the ratings get sorted into kinds of failure. The kinds that keep coming back become agent evaluations (#53). Phoenix can also turn rated spans into a dataset, which is what its experiments run on.

Phoenix's own UI can already rate a trace, but that means finding the turn in Phoenix later. From the chat, it's one click. Links from the chat to each turn's trace, and to the session, let Joe go from what he sees in the chat to how the coordinator got there. They take the place of the raw view, which #141 removes.

An **annotation** is a rating that Phoenix keeps on a span or a session: a name, a label, a score, a note, and who made it. A **session** in Phoenix groups a chat's turns by their `session.id`. That's the **agent session ID**, the Agent SDK's ID for the conversation (`agentSessionId` in `src/persistence/session.ts`), not the app's own session ID, which the page uses (systems design section 10).

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 10.1 (the chat view).
- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), sections 4 (what the stream sends the browser) and 10 (traces, and how Phoenix is reached).
- Phoenix 20.26.0's source, at the [`arize-phoenix-v20.26.0`](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/tree/arize-phoenix-v20.26.0) tag: the redirect links in `js/app/src/Routes.tsx`, and the annotation routes in `src/phoenix/server/api/routers/v1/spans.py`, `sessions.py`, and `annotations.py`. Through the tunnel, Phoenix's own API docs are at `http://127.0.0.1:6006/docs`.

Agreed in chat on 2026-10-26:

- **Each reply gets a thumbs up and a thumbs down, and so does the whole session.** Either one opens a box for a note. Good turns get rated as well as bad ones.
- **Each reply gets a "View trace" link, and the chat gets a "View session" link.** Each opens Phoenix in a new tab. Phoenix 20.26 has redirect links that take our own IDs, so the app doesn't look anything up in Phoenix. `/redirects/spans/<span ID>` opens the trace with that span picked, so a turn's link needs only its turn span's ID. `/redirects/sessions/<session ID>` opens the session, and takes the agent session ID.
- **The browser never talks to Phoenix.** On the server, the browser can't reach it. So the page sends a rating to the app, under `/api`, and the app posts it to Phoenix, the way it sends traces. It posts with `fetch`, like the health check in `src/tracing/phoenix.ts`, not with a new package.
- **The links work only on Joe's machine, with the SSH tunnel up** (DEVELOPMENT.md section 2), since Phoenix's UI is at `http://127.0.0.1:6006` there and nowhere else.

What Phoenix 20.26 offers, from its source:

- `POST /v1/span_annotations` and `POST /v1/session_annotations` save annotations. Each one has a `name`, an `annotator_kind` of `HUMAN`, `CODE`, or `LLM`, a `result` with a `label`, a `score`, and an `explanation`, `metadata`, and an `identifier`.
- When an annotation with the same name and `identifier` is already there, Phoenix updates it in place of adding one.
- By default, Phoenix queues an annotation and replies at once. An annotation for a span or session it doesn't have yet is tried again every 10 seconds, up to 60 times, and then dropped with no error (`src/phoenix/db/insertion/span_annotation.py`, `session_annotation.py`, and `constants.py`). With `?sync=true`, it saves it before replying, and refuses one for a span it doesn't have, with a 404.
- The `/redirects/...` links aren't server redirects. Phoenix replies with its web page, and the page's own code asks Phoenix's GraphQL API which trace or session the ID belongs to (`getSpanByOtelId` and `getProjectSessionById`, in `js/app/src/pages/redirects/`). Then it moves the browser there.

## Open questions

- ~~What does a rating hold? A first guess is the name `rating`, the label `up` or `down`, the score 1 or 0, the note as the explanation, and `annotator_kind` `HUMAN`.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: as guessed. The name is `rating` for both turns and sessions, the label `up` or `down`, the score 1 or 0, the note as the explanation (left out when there's none), and `annotator_kind` `HUMAN`. Systems design section 10.
- ~~Can a rating be changed, such as from up to down? If so, the `identifier` could be the user's ID, so each user has one rating per turn and per session.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: yes. The `identifier` is the rater's user ID, so a new rating replaces that user's earlier one on the same turn or session. A rating can be flipped, not taken back. Functional spec 10.1, systems design section 10.
- ~~Who sees the trace and session links? Only Joe can open them. The app has no way to tell Joe from other users. One choice is to show them to everyone. Another is an environment value with Joe's user ID, which the page would learn through `/api/me` (`src/shared/me.schema.ts`).~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: everyone. For anyone else, they're dead links, which is harmless. The span ID and agent session ID aren't secret. Functional spec 10.1.
- ~~Who can rate? If any signed-in user can, the route checks that the user owns the session, as other session routes do (`src/api/owned.ts`). It can't check that a span ID belongs to that session, unless it asks Phoenix.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: any signed-in user, on a session they own. The route checks ownership with `ownedSession()`, and that a span ID is 16 hex characters. It doesn't check that the span belongs to the session. For a session rating, the page sends no ID, and the server finds the agent session ID itself. Systems design section 4.
- ~~What happens when a rating comes before the turn's span reaches Phoenix? Spans are sent in batches every few seconds, and the turn span ends only after the reply does. With `sync=true`, Phoenix refuses it with a 404. Without it, check whether Phoenix keeps a queued annotation for a span it doesn't have yet. On a new chat's first turn, the session may not be in Phoenix yet either.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: post without `sync=true`, and let Phoenix's queue cover the delay (see "What Phoenix 20.26 offers" above). The app adds no retry or wait. A rating on a span that never reaches Phoenix is dropped after about 10 minutes, with no error. If the app can't reach Phoenix, the page says the rating wasn't saved. The local check confirms a rating sent at once is kept. Systems design section 10.
- ~~Which turns can be rated and linked? The page gets a turn's span ID only for turns it streamed. A resumed session's earlier turns come from the transcript, which has no span IDs. So do turns the page shows after waiting on a turn that was already running when it loaded (`turnRunning` in `web/src/chat-state.ts`). A turn whose SDK call threw has no span ID either. The session's rating and link need only the agent session ID, which the server always has, so they work in every case.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: only turns the page streamed. Turns loaded from the transcript get no thumbs and no link. They can be rated in Phoenix's own UI, from the session link. A turn whose SDK call threw does get a span ID, since the turn span is made before the SDK call, and the span ID is the turn's first event. The session's thumbs and link show once the session exists. Functional spec 10.1.
- ~~Where do the thumbs go on a failed turn with no reply? Failed turns are the ones most worth rating down.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: each streamed turn gets a row under its last card, with the thumbs and "View trace". With no reply, that's under the user's message. A failed turn's row also says "The reply didn't finish.", so it still makes sense once the page's error line is gone. Functional spec 10.1.
- ~~Where does the page get Phoenix's address for the links? It could be written into the page as `http://127.0.0.1:6006`, or come from a `VITE_` value in `web/src/web-env.schema.ts`. The app's `PHOENIX_URL` won't do, since on the server it's `http://phoenix:6006`.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: a constant in the page's code, since the browser reaches Phoenix through the tunnel at the same address, locally and on the live site. Systems design section 10.

## Do

- **Send each turn's span ID to the browser,** as the turn's first event, before the SDK call. `TurnTrace` (`src/agent/turn-trace.ts`) keeps the turn span private, and it's created in `runTurnWithSdk` (`src/agent/coordinator.ts`), so this means a way to read the span ID from it, and a change to `TurnEvent` (`src/agent/turn-event.ts`). Update the fake turn runner (`src/agent/run-turn.fake.ts`), `npm run chat`'s event printer (`src/chat.ts`), and `chatEventOf()` (`src/api/turn-stream.ts`) to match.
- **Send the page the agent session ID,** for the session link. Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: add it to the `session` event and to the resume reply (`SessionResponse` in `src/shared/session.schema.ts`), next to the app's session ID. A link can't go through the app to look it up, since a link click doesn't carry the sign-in token. The session rating route looks it up on the server.
- **Add an `/api` route that saves a rating** for a turn or a session. Put its input schema in `src/shared/`, and check it with Zod. Post the annotation to Phoenix from a new dependency in `ApiDependencies` (`src/api/api.ts`), set up in `src/main.ts`. Test it with `fetch` faked, as `src/tracing/phoenix.test.ts` does.
- **Add the ratings, the note box, and the links to the chat page.**
- **Start the session's thumbs with the user's last rating of it,** and the note box with its note, read from Phoenix when the chat opens. Added on 2026-10-26, in chat, so a session rated earlier doesn't show blank thumbs that would overwrite its rating. Turns stay as settled: replies loaded from history get no thumbs.
- **Write it down,** in functional spec 10.1, and systems design sections 4 and 10.
- **Check it locally,** with the tunnel up. Sign in as Claude Code's own user (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5). Send a chat turn to `npm run dev` through `/api`. Rate the turn at once, before its span is sent, and rate the session. Read the annotations back with Phoenix's REST API. Check each link's ID by asking Phoenix's GraphQL API the same question its redirect page asks (`getSpanByOtelId`, `getProjectSessionById`), and checking it gives the turn's trace and the chat's session. Then, in Chrome through Claude in Chrome, rate a reply and the session from the page, and open both links.

## Done when

- `npm run check` passes.
- Locally, with the tunnel up, a thumbs up with a note on a turn, sent through `/api` right after the turn ends, shows on that turn's span in Phoenix's `road-trip-agent-local` project, with its label and note. A thumbs down on the session shows on the session.
- Phoenix's GraphQL API finds the turn's trace from the span ID in its link, and the chat's session from the agent session ID in the session link.
- From the page in Chrome, a rating on a reply and on the session shows in Phoenix, and both links open the right trace and session.
- Reopening a rated session in Chrome shows its rating chosen, and its note in the note box.
- In the PR review, Joe rates a reply and the session from the page, and opens both links.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.
title: Rate and annotate chat turns and sessions, with links to their traces

body:
## Why

`npm run check` fails locally whenever a Claude Code session has a git worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, such as `.claude/worktrees/itinerary-read-size`. ESLint runs on `.`, so it lints the worktree's files too. Each one fails with "Parsing error: No tsconfigRootDir was set, and multiple candidate TSConfigRootDirs are present", since the worktree has its own `tsconfig.json`. The pre-commit hook runs the check, so no commit can be made in the main checkout while such a worktree exists. Git already ignores `.claude/worktrees/` (`.gitignore`), and CI's check runs on a clean checkout, so only local runs are hit. Prettier runs only on `src` and `web`, and Vitest found no tests there, so only ESLint needs the change.

It came up while making #144. That commit skipped the hook with `LEFTHOOK=0`, after format, types, lint on `src web *.config.ts`, and the tests were each run by hand and passed.

## Design

- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), sections 1 (the one check) and 6 (config files change only with Joe's approval).

## Open questions

None yet.

## Do

- **Add `.claude/worktrees/` to `globalIgnores()` in `eslint.config.mjs`,** and to the comment above it, saying a Claude Code session's worktree is a full copy of the repo. This is a config file, so it needs Joe's approval (DEVELOPMENT.md section 6).

## Done when

- With a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, `npm run check` passes in the main checkout.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR.
title: ESLint lints Claude Code's worktrees under .claude/worktrees, so the local check fails

body:
**Starts** once #53 is done, since it needs agent evaluations. Building the change also needs trip versions (#243).

## Why

After a resume, the coordinator reads the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory again before changing anything (technical spec 5.2). The read gives the trip as it stands now, but it doesn't say what changed since the transcript ends. Three things can change: another session edited the trip, a worker saved candidates before a restart cut off the turn, or another session's writes reported warnings. To find them, the coordinator has to compare the fresh read with an older read far back in its transcript, plus every write it made since. That's a hard comparison for a model to get right.

The idea: on a resume, give the coordinator the current itinerary and also a list or summary of what changed since the session's last turn. Then it has the current state, and doesn't have to work out the changes itself.

It gets more pressing if a whole read stops listing candidates, as the research doc for #129 proposes. The coordinator would then see only a count, such as "Candidates: 3 in set 1," on a stop that had none. Nothing would tell it that the user never heard about them.

**This is a guess about the coordinator, not a seen problem.** So it goes by evidence. Before anything is designed or built, an agent evaluation (#53) has to show that the coordinator really misses changes after a resume. If it doesn't, the idea is dropped. If it does, the same evaluation shows whether the change fixes it.

## Design

- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2: the rule "When a session is resumed".
- [Persistence design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/persistence.md), sections 7 and 8.5: a cut-off turn, and how a resume works.
- [Research doc: making a whole itinerary read smaller](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md) (`research/itinerary-read-size.md`), section 2: why the coordinator reads the whole trip.

## Open questions

- What counts as a change worth listing: stays, stops, picks, candidates, approvals, rejected places, check results, the trip brief?
- How does code know what changed? The itinerary keeps no history today. It could keep versions, or a log of changes with their times. #243 saves a trip version at the start of each turn. Comparing the trip now with the version from the start of the session's last turn would also list the coordinator's own changes in that turn, so this may need a version at the end of each turn too. Added on 2026-11-02, when #243 was opened.
- What marks "since the last turn": the time of the session's last saved transcript line, or something else?
- Is it a list from code, or a summary? A list from code fits the rule that code works out what the model doesn't need to.
- Does it come with the read, or in the line the app adds to the first message after a resume?

## Do

- Write an agent evaluation (#53) that resumes a session after each kind of change in Why: another session's edit, candidates from a cut-off worker, and warnings another session's writes reported. It checks whether the coordinator notices each change, and tells the user about it when it should. Run it on the itinerary read as it is at the time.
- Put the results in the issue.
- If the coordinator misses changes, propose an answer for each open question. Otherwise, propose dropping the idea.

## Done when

- The evaluation is in the repo, and its results are in the issue.
- Joe has agreed to an approach, and it's written into technical spec 5.2, or the idea is dropped.
- An issue is opened to build it, if it needs building.

## Ends in

A decision.

**Settled in:** chat.
title: Tell the coordinator what changed since its last turn, on a resume

body:
## Why

Once a stay's tier is set, it should stay as it is until the user asks to change it. Today the app revisits it when the stay's nights change. Example: Moab is picked at mid-range as a 3-night stay, under the rule "mid-range for stays of 2+ nights". The user cuts Moab to 1 night. A check note then says "Moab's nights changed from 3 to 1. Its tier was set for 3," and the coordinator asks whether to keep the hotel or see value options (technical spec section 9).

That's inconsistent with how rules work. Nothing revisits a meal's tier or a stay's tier when the user changes a budget rule or the default tier. Joe decided on 2026-10-26, in chat, that both work the same way: a change to the rules or to a stay's nights applies only to tiers set after it. Nothing already set is revisited. The user sees each tier in the itinerary view, and asks for a change if they want one.

So the note, and the code that exists only to raise it, go. That's less deterministic code, and one less rule for the coordinator to follow.

## Design

- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 9 (the paragraph "A stay's tier records the nights it was set for"), and the check table in section 8 (the row "Stay tier set for different nights").
- [Domain model](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/domain-model.md): the stay's `tierSetForNightCount` property, its "Tier and nights" paragraph, `setTier()`, and the `stayTierSetForDifferentNights` check kind and its row in the check results table.
- [Research doc: making a whole itinerary read smaller](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md) (`research/itinerary-read-size.md`), section 5: the whole read proposed for #129 already leaves out the tier's rule and the nights it was set for.

## Open questions

- ~~Saved trips hold `tierSetForNightCount` in each stay of their plan document, and the plan schema is strict (`staySchema` in `src/persistence/itinerary-plan.schema.ts`). So once the field is removed, a saved trip would fail to load. How should saved trips be handled: a one-off update of the saved rows, or a schema that still accepts the key and drops it?~~ Settled 2026-10-26 in PR #149: a one-off update, migration 0008, which also removes saved results of the removed check.

## Do

- Remove the `stayTierSetForDifferentNights` check and its note, and `tierSetForNightCount` on the stay, from the code and its tests. The code is in `src/domain/check-kind.ts`, `check-result.ts`, `stay-checks.ts`, `stay.ts`, `src/persistence/itinerary-document.ts`, `itinerary-plan.schema.ts`, and `src/tools/day-lines.ts`, which writes "set when the stay had N nights" on the "Lodging tier:" line.
- Handle saved trips, as settled in the open question.
- In technical spec section 9, replace the paragraph on nights with the rule above: a change to the rules or to a stay's nights applies only to tiers set after it, and nothing already set is revisited. Remove the check table row in section 8.
- Remove the same parts from the domain model.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, in case a tool description or the coordinator's view file names the note.

## Done when

- The note, the check, and `tierSetForNightCount` are gone from the code, the tests, and the design docs.
- Technical spec section 9 states the rule.
- A saved trip from before the change still loads.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR.
title: Don't revisit a stay's tier when its nights change

body:
**Starts** once #150 and #148 are merged. #150 writes the design. #148 changes the "Lodging tier:" line in `src/tools/day-lines.ts`, which this issue changes too.

## Why

The coordinator can't read the whole itinerary of a long trip. A whole `read_itinerary` of a busy 14-day trip is about 34,500 tokens. That's over Claude Code's limit of 25,000 tokens for a tool result, so the tool refuses it. The coordinator reads the whole trip at the start of each session, after a resume, and for "what's left to decide?" (technical spec 5.2). So on a trip longer than about a week, it gets an error in all three.

#129 settled on a whole read that gives less. It gives each picked place with its town, and counts the other candidates by set. It leaves out the rationale, the weather text, and the rule behind each tier, which the itinerary view shows the user. That brings the busy trip to about 15,300 tokens. Reads of a day, stay, or stop don't change.

## Design

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1: the `read_itinerary` row, and the sections "A whole read gives less than a scoped read", "A read has a size limit of 25,000 tokens", "A trip too large to read whole can't be planned any further", and "A scoped read too large to return gets a different error".
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2 ("What a whole read gives") and 7.2 ("Reading the itinerary").
- For a longer example of the format than tool design 2.1 gives, `research/itinerary-read-size/slim-read-proposed.txt` is a whole 14-day trip in it, with its last stay still undecided. It's a mockup, written by a script, so where it and tool design 2.1 differ, tool design 2.1 wins.

## Open questions

- None.

## Do

- Change the whole read, `wholeLines()` in `src/tools/itinerary-lines.ts`, to the format in tool design 2.1. The lines are built in `src/tools/day-lines.ts` and `src/tools/stop-lines.ts`, at a level of detail, `"short"` or `"full"`. Today the whole read and a day read both use `dayLines(…, "short")`. The day read doesn't change, so the whole read needs a third level of detail, not a change to `"short"`. `stayLines(…, "short")` is used only by the whole read.
- These details of the format aren't spelled out in tool design 2.1:
  - **The town** comes from the same rule the short line uses, `townOf()` in `src/domain/place.ts`, which is private today. Expose it, such as with a `town` getter. A place with no town, such as a trail whose address has none, shows only its name and ID.
  - **The folded stop line** gives, after the name and ID: the town, then the detour time, then the visit time, as in `Selected: Valley of Fire State Park (place_…), Overton, detour 38 m when offered, visit time 2 h.` The detour time is the selected place's candidate's `detourTimeInMinutes`, and is left out when it's null.
  - **A count line** names each set with at least one candidate to count, in set order, counted from 1 (`setNumber + 1`), such as `3 in set 1, 2 in set 2.` For "Other candidates:", the selected place isn't counted, and a set left with none is skipped. With nothing left to count, there's no line. Today's `- Candidates:` and `- Lodging candidates:` blocks become one count line each, in the same place: indented under a stop, and at the stay's level for lodging.
  - **No candidates:** a stay with no lodging candidates keeps today's `Lodging: no candidates yet.`, and a stop with none keeps `No candidates yet.` on its stop line. Neither gets a count line.
- Split the error for a reply over the limit, `TOO_LARGE_ERROR` in `src/tools/itinerary-tools.ts`, in two. A whole read gets "Can't read the itinerary: it's too large to read, so this trip can't be planned any further." A day, stay, or stop read keeps today's text.
- Rewrite the tool's description, `READ_ITINERARY_DESCRIPTION`, to match tool design 2.1. "Candidates are listed in the order offered, with their set" and "read it a stay at a time instead" are no longer true of a whole read.
- Update the comment on `MAXIMUM_REPLY_CHARACTERS` to the measurement in tool design 2.1.
- Add two of the rules in technical spec 5.2, "What a whole read gives", to the coordinator's instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`): read a stop or stay before talking through or recommending its options, and for "why did we pick that?" or a stay's weather text. The third rule, on "More options" and the tier buttons, goes in with #62, which adds those actions.
- Change the tests:
  - `src/tools/itinerary-read-marks.test.ts` has a test that a whole read of `fourteenDayExample` is refused as too large. In the new format, it should fit. So that test reads it whole and expects a reply. A new test checks each error: a whole read over the limit gets the new error, and a scoped read over it gets today's. Build whatever trip is needed to go over the limit, such as one with more candidates.
  - A new test pins the new lines: the two count lines ("Candidates:" and "Other candidates:"), "No candidates yet.", the selected place folded into a stop line and into a "Lodging:" line, "Lodging: none selected yet." with "Lodging candidates:", the weather line without its text, still marked out of date when it is, and a tier line without its rule.
  - Tests of day, stay, and stop reads pass unchanged.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.

#152 may be built at the same time. Both change the coordinator's instructions and its view file. Whichever merges second rebases onto `main` and runs `npm run agent-views` again.

## Done when

- A whole read of `fourteenDayExample` (`src/domain/fourteen-day-example.fake.ts`) comes back in the new format, not refused. The PR gives its length in characters.
- Each error is given in its case, and a test checks both.
- The new lines are pinned by a test, and reads of a day, stay, or stop are unchanged.
- The coordinator's view file shows the new description and instructions.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR.
title: Make the whole itinerary read smaller

body:
**Starts** once #150 is merged, which writes the design.

## Why

#151 makes a whole `read_itinerary` smaller by listing no candidate names, only a count for each stop and stay. Then nothing in the coordinator's context tells it which stop or stay holds a candidate the user names, such as "let's do the Desert Pearl."

A wrong guess fails quietly. `select_user_place` on another stop adds the place there as one the user named, and the stop that offered it stays undecided. `find_place` doesn't help either. It searches Google, not the trip, so a typo such as "Desert Rose" can return a real Desert Rose somewhere else, and never the Desert Pearl Inn.

`find_in_trip` searches the trip's own places by name, with string similarity, and says where each one sits in the trip. It costs tokens only when the user names a place, not on every whole read.

## Design

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1: the `find_in_trip` row, and the section "`find_in_trip` finds a place the user names". Section 3: who gets it.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), sections 5.1, 5.2 ("When the user names a place"), and 7.1.

## Open questions

- None.

## Do

- Add `find_in_trip` to `createTripServer()` in `src/tools/trip-server.ts`, with the read-only annotation `read_itinerary` has. The coordinator already gets every tool on the `trip` server (`allowedTools` in `src/agent/coordinator.ts`), so it needs no other change to reach it. No worker gets it (tool design section 3).
- Its one input is the text, a required string, named `text` as in `find_place`'s input (`src/tools/place-input.schema.ts`).
- Load the trip as `read_itinerary` does, with `session.reader.read(session.tripId)` (`src/tools/itinerary-tools.ts`). Search the places the itinerary holds: every stop's and stay's candidates, the rejected places, the start and end places, and the stays' towns. Not the trip's other saved places, which come from searches and were never offered. Each place is listed once, however many spots hold it.
- Match by trigram similarity, written in TypeScript in the tool, with no new package. Lowercase both strings, and take out punctuation and a leading "the", before scoring. Score and break ties as tool design 2.1 says. It always returns the 5 closest, or every place when the trip has fewer. Use `FIND_PLACE_MATCHES` in `src/tools/place-tools.ts` for the 5, since the two tools return the same number. There's no cutoff for a match.
- Write the reply in the format in tool design 2.1. Its first line gives the number returned, such as "The 3 places in the trip closest to "Desert Rose", best first:" on a smaller trip. The lines for each spot, in the order the whole read lists them:
  - `Lodging candidate for Stay 1, Springdale (stay_…), set 1. Selected.` or `Not selected.`
  - `Candidate for Day 12, Stop 5 (stop_…), attraction: "the east end of the South Rim", set 1. Selected.` or `Not selected.`
  - `Rejected for the whole trip: "too far off the route".`
  - `The start place.`, `The end place.`, or, for a loop, `The start and end place.`
  - `The town of Stay 1 (stay_…).`
- The tool's description says it searches only this trip's places, and always returns the closest few, so the coordinator checks that one is the place the user meant. Write the text that names where a place sits, such as `Candidate for Day 12, Stop 5 (stop_…), attraction: "the east end of the South Rim", set 1. Not selected.`, as a function `select_user_place` can use too. #56 gives `select_user_place`'s reply a line in the same form, for each other stop or stay where the place is a candidate. If #56 is merged first and already has such a function, use it here instead of writing a second one.
- Add the rule in technical spec 5.2, "When the user names a place", to the coordinator's instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`).
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.

#151 may be built at the same time. Both change the coordinator's instructions and its view file. Whichever merges second rebases onto `main` and runs `npm run agent-views` again.

## Done when

- Tests show these, on a small trip built in the test with the place names below. The example trips' places are made up, so they don't have these names.
  - "Desert Rose" ranks the Desert Pearl Inn first, ahead of Desert View Watchtower and Rose Well Camp.
  - "Cliffrose" ranks "Cliffrose Springdale, Curio Collection by Hilton" first, ahead of Cliff Palace.
  - Case, punctuation, and a leading "the" don't change the match.
  - A place in two spots, such as a hotel that's also a dinner candidate, gets a line for each.
  - A selected candidate, a rejected place, the start and end place, and a stay's town each get their own line.
  - A place saved by a search but never offered isn't returned.
  - A trip with fewer than 5 places returns all of them, and a trip with none says so, with no error.
- The coordinator's view file shows the new tool and its instructions.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR.
title: Find a place in the trip by name: find_in_trip

and

title: Shorter response when trip brief or itinerary has not been set yet

body:
## Why

The coordinator's instructions and tool descriptions grew one issue at a time. Read together, in the coordinator's view file (`src/agent/coordinator.view.md`), they have gaps that make the agent's job harder than it needs to be, whatever model runs it. This issue collects those gaps, from Joe's review of the view file and an independent review of it, so they're fixed in one PR.

The bar for an item: a fix that's clearly good practice goes in here, with no evaluation needed first. That covers things a person using the same tools would need too, such as knowing what the app's terms mean. An item whose benefit is in doubt, such as one that adds tokens to every turn for a gain no one is sure of, isn't fixed here. It becomes a candidate for an agent evaluation instead.

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 4: the app's terms.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2: what the coordinator's instructions cover.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md): the tool descriptions.

## Items

1. **The app's terms aren't defined for the coordinator.** The instructions define anchors and stretches (technical spec 4.1), but not the terms from functional spec 4 that the tools are built on: stay, night, day, last day, leg, stop, and candidate. The model pieces them together from tool descriptions. Example: `add_stay` says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights", and a rule says "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day". The riskiest gap is how nights and days add up. A 3-night stay covers three days, and the last day has no night, so a 7-day trip has 6 nights of stays. Nothing tells the model this. It could add 7 nights for a 7-day trip and get 8 days. The trip length check would catch it, but the model would be fixing a mistake it didn't need to make.

   The lines an itinerary read returns aren't explained either. Tool design section 4 says what an item means goes in the agent's instructions, and a read's lines are explained by the instructions. The trip brief follows this: the instructions explain each item, so `read_trip_brief` stays short. Nothing does the same for the itinerary. In a read of a day, nothing explains "in set 1", "Along the leg" or "Near the Springdale stay", "detour 38 m when offered", "with the drive buffer", "free time", or "Set time: 6:30 p.m." The `read_itinerary` description itself is fine. It says what each scope returns, which is specific to that tool.

   A few more terms need a line. "Set" as a noun ("2 in set 1") is one batch of candidates, and the option card shows only the newest set (functional spec 7.5). Without that, the coordinator may recommend a set 1 candidate the user can't see on the card. "Search area" is where a stop's places are looked for. "Last day" means the trip's final day in the check results rule, but the rule on removing a night says "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day," meaning the last of that stay's days. Say that one another way. Drive time is named three ways: "drive time" in the planning rounds, "road time" in `set_waypoints` and the reads, and "driving with the drive buffer" in the reads. Say what each is, so the model compares the right one with comfortableDrivingInHours.

   One repeat goes the other way. The bullets under "Reading the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory" say a whole read leaves out the rationale and the weather text, which the `read_itinerary` description already says. Tool design section 4 says the system prompt never repeats a tool's description.

   Fix: add a section on the itinerary to the instructions, like the one on the trip brief. It defines the terms, drawn from functional spec 4, and says what each line of a read means. Drop the repeat from the reading bullets, and keep the rules there on when to read a stop or stay. Add the section to the list in technical spec 5.2.

   Then review every tool description against the new section, so each term is defined in one place and used the same way everywhere. `compute_route` needs it most. Its description says "A stop is where the party stops, such as a town that might become a stay," and its points take a kind of "stop" or "passThrough". In the itinerary, a stop is a meal or attraction on a day, not a town. It also says "pass-through point" where `set_waypoints` says "waypoint" for the same idea.

2. **The rule for places the user names says to always call `find_in_trip` first, with no reason given.** `find_in_trip` exists because a whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so the coordinator doesn't know their names. The rule leaves that out, and it's broader than technical spec 7.1, which says to look up only "a name it can't find in context." As written, it sends the coordinator to `find_in_trip` for a place it already has an ID for, such as a selected restaurant from the whole read, and for a place that's clearly new to the trip. It also says to ask the user when no match is clearly the place, which fits a typo such as "Desert Rose", but not a place that isn't in the trip. `find_in_trip` always returns the 5 closest places, so when the user says "let's add Arches" on a trip with no Arches, none is close, and the rule has the coordinator ask "Did you mean Desert View Watchtower?" Fix: give the reason, and split the rule into three cases. For a place the coordinator already has an ID for, use it. For a place it doesn't have, that may be one the trip offered, use `find_in_trip`. Ask the user when a match is close but may not be the place. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so use `find_place`. For a place that's new to the trip, use `find_place`. Skipping `find_in_trip` for a new place is safe, since `select_user_place` refuses a place that's already a candidate on that stop, and its reply names any other stop or stay where the place is a candidate. Proposed wording, to replace the first bullet under "Places the user names" and change the second:

   > A whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so you won't know their names unless a scoped read or a worker's reply showed them.
   > - When the user names a place you already have an ID for, use it.
   > - When they name one you don't have, and it may be a place the trip offered, look for it with find_in_trip. When a match is close but you aren't sure it's the place, ask the user, such as "Did you mean the Desert Pearl Inn, the hotel in Springdale?" for "Desert Rose". A shorter form of a name, such as "the Desert Pearl" for the Desert Pearl Inn, is clear, so don't ask. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so look it up with find_place.
   > - For a place that's new to the trip, such as one a friend recommended, use find_place.

   Change technical spec 5.2 ("When the user names a place") and tool design 2.1 ("`find_in_trip` finds a place the user names") to match.

3. **The rule on when to raise warnings is unclear.** It says "Raise warnings at the end of the turn, for those still open, once no change is still being discussed with the user." "At the end of the turn" sounds like every turn, and "a change" is vague. It could be read as holding warnings until the whole trip is planned. It means holding them until the change the coordinator and the user are working on is settled, which can take several turns. The weather worker rule in technical spec 5.2 uses the same phrase and has an example. The coordinator's line has none. Fix: replace the line with this wording, and change technical spec 5.2 ("How to handle broken feasibility rules") to match:

   > Raise warnings once a change is settled, not while you and the user are still working it out. A change can take several turns, such as adding a night and then going through the stops it moved. Raise them at the end of the turn where the user confirms the change or backs out of it, and only those still open. Example: adding a Big Sur night makes a 3-day trip 4 days. Don't raise the trip length while you're still going through the stops the night moved. If the user then removes the night, the warning is gone, and there's nothing to raise.

4. **`add_stay`'s description says where the stay goes in a way that only makes sense next to the input schema.** It says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights, after the stay given or first." "The stay given" and "first" point to the `after` input without naming it, and "first" isn't quoted, though the input's description quotes it. The next sentence uses "first" again, with another meaning: "Needs the itinerary's start place, end place, and start date first." Fix: name the input, and say what "first" does. A starting point:

   > Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights. Give after the ID of the stay it follows, or "first" to put it before every other stay. The place is usually a town. The itinerary's start place, end place, and start date must be set before a stay can be added.

   Check `update_stay`'s "where it goes" the same way. `add_stops` and `move_stop` aren't built yet, but take an `after` input too (tool design 2.1, "Where an item goes"). Add a line to tool design 2.1 that a description names the `after` input and says what "first" does, so they follow the same pattern.

5. **`update_day`'s start time takes "none" to mean the trip brief's usual start time.** "None" reads as "no start time," which isn't what it does. The day still starts at the usual start time. Fix: take "default" instead, for a day's start time only. A stop's set time keeps "none" (tool design 2.1, "Times are clock times"), since a stop with no set time really has none. Today only the start time uses `NO_TIME` in `src/tools/skeleton-input.schema.ts`, since the stop tools aren't built yet. Rename it for "default", and change tool design 2.1 to match.

6. **`find_place`'s description says "When you aren't sure where the place is, give its state."** The sentence is about the `where` input, but doesn't name it. It means: when you don't know the town, give the state rather than guess a town. It reads as if the state were optional. And `where` takes "a town, region, or state," so a region with no state, such as "Big Sur", is allowed, though it's the case where the state helps most. The app plans only US trips, so every place has a state. Fix: drop the sentence from the description, and say it in `where`'s input description instead. A starting point:

   > A town or region with its state, or only the state when you aren't sure where the place is, such as "Moab, UT", "Big Sur, CA", or "Utah".

   Change the `find_place` row in tool design 2.3 to match.

7. **The instructions describe a write's check results differently from what the tools return.** "Tools that change the trip" says each write "replies with the feasibility check results the change made new, changed, or gone, anywhere in the trip." The reply (`src/tools/check-results-reply.ts`) also lists the already-known results for what the write touched, and marks a warning the user approved as "approved", such as "New warning, approved: …". The instructions never say what "approved" means, what "open" means in "warnings that are still open", or that a warning must be raised while a note is the coordinator's call (technical spec 8). Example: after a write, the coordinator sees "New warning, approved: Day 4 drives 7 h", and raises a warning the user already accepted. Fix: say what the reply lists, as technical spec 8 does ("What comes back"). Say each result is a warning or a note: a warning must be raised, and whether to mention a note is up to the coordinator. Say a warning marked approved is one the user accepted, so it isn't open, and isn't raised again.

8. **The memory section contradicts itself.** It says user memory holds standing preferences "such as their usual driving hours, route preference, budget, meal habits". Then "Writing memory" says "Don't save what the trip brief or the itinerary holds", and the trip brief holds those items for this trip. Example: the user says "we never drive more than 5 hours, on any trip." The coordinator sets comfortableDrivingInHours and skips user memory, so the next trip doesn't know. The rule is meant for trip memory. Fix: make it "Don't save to trip memory what the trip brief or the itinerary holds". The rule is only in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, so add it to the "Writing memory" bullets in technical spec 5.2 too.
