```
lodgingPreferencesText: mid-range in moab, cheap in torrey
```

The start, the end, and October 11 are in the itinerary. Stargazing isn't a must-see in the brief, since the simulated user gave it only as a time, "capitol reef around 1 a.m." It's a stop at Panorama Point. The 4 hours of driving came from the user memory left by the San Francisco run, and matches the trip file. Day 2 starts at 5:30 and the last day at 10:00.

**Refused tool calls:** none.

### The first run, kept on purpose

Trip `trip_vmpunync`, on 2026-11-04 from 22:28 to 22:41 UTC. App sessions `session_q65v3uxk` and `session_wgfb2fvh`, Phoenix sessions `30d5cb5b-1268-4de3-b9ca-bda17f574824` and `893d0dba-8da9-4af1-b5b2-625a33cef40e`.

At change 5, the simulated user asked for the hike, and the planner offered three ways to fit it. It answered "no, keep the windows and corona. can the five hours include delicate arch and the windows?" The planner said yes, so no hike was added, and the planner never had to rework Day 2. The instructions say to see each change through, so this run fails that check. The trip still got fully planned: both hotels and every stop are picked, no cards are open, and the planner named nothing left to decide.

The planner handled this well. The simulated user backed out, because the persona says favorites aren't up for debate, and change 5 didn't say the hike outranks them. I added that to `trips/moab.md`, in the PR for this issue. Joe decided on 2026-11-04 to keep this run for the evaluations, since a user who pushes back is a different scenario from the second run. So its sessions have no `not_for_evaluation` annotation.

One `add_stop_candidates` call was refused in this run, for sending `visitTimeInMinutes`. That's the same refusal as #266.

### How Codex played the user differently from Claude Code (#68)

- **More looking.** Codex ran `itinerary` 17 times, against 4 for Claude Code. This matches the San Francisco runs.
- **Fewer clicks.** Codex clicked Select 3 times and left the rest to one message. Claude Code clicked 10 times, and named some picks in the chat.
- **About the same number of facts at once.** The middle message was 14 words for Codex and 13 for Claude Code. Claude Code's longest was 31 words, and Codex's 21. So `curt` closed the gap the San Francisco runs showed.
- **Must-sees.** Codex answered the planner's must-see question, so three of the four are in the brief. Claude Code never answered it, so its brief has none of them by name.
- **The 5-hour hike.** Both took Devils Garden and dropped Love Muffin. Claude Code dropped the Windows and kept Corona Arch. Codex moved the Windows to Day 1 and dropped Corona Arch. Only Codex backed out of the hike, in its first run. Claude Code saw it through on the old wording.
- **The page's labels.** Codex read the "Out of date" label on Moab's weather advice and said so, and the planner reran the weather worker. Claude Code's messages never raised it.
- **A shorter final note.** Codex gave the IDs and one problem. Claude Code went through each change.

The two runs took about the same time, 14 minutes.

### Worth knowing for the evaluations

- **Weather advice left out of date.** After change 5, the coordinator didn't mention or refresh Moab's advice, which still named Corona Arch. The label and the `weatherOutOfDate` note worked as designed. It refreshed only when the user asked.
- **Old reasoning caught.** In session 2, the coordinator said two parts of the hotel's reason were out of date: the rest day, and the 5:45 start. The hotel's "Why" still says "ideal for the no-driving rest day."
- **A stop that kept an old length or name.** The Windows stop says "about 2 hours" but has 1 h 15 m. The Torrey check-in says "before dinner," but it now comes after.
- **An order changed on purpose.** The user said to check in first. The coordinator put dinner first, and said why.

### App bugs

None found, so no issues were filed.

title: Record the Moab trip with Codex

body:
## Why

Google routes a drive by today's road conditions, not the trip's dates. A trip planned months ahead sees the roads that are closed when it's planned. Seasonal road closures are out of scope (functional spec, section 5 and section 6.1), so the app assumes the roads it routes on are the trip's roads. A closure that's over by the trip breaks that.

In the Montana run on the live site (#273), planned on 2026-11-05 for September 13 to 18, 2027, Google treated Yellowstone's inner roads and Going-to-the-Sun Road as closed for winter:

- **Drive times were false.** It routed around the park. Day 2, Gardiner to Old Faithful by way of Lamar Valley, showed 8½ to 14½ hours of driving, where the coordinator put the real September drive at 3½ to 4 hours. Day 3 showed about 8 hours, against about 2½. The schedule had Lamar Valley at 10:54 a.m. instead of dawn, and dinners after 10 p.m. The driving and opening-hours checks flagged these days all through the session.
- **A must-see couldn't be added.** `select_user_place` for Logan Pass was refused 3 times, with "Google found no driving route ... through Logan Pass Visitor Center". `compute_route` was refused twice when the coordinator first sketched routes through Lamar Valley and Logan Pass. The trip ended with Logan Pass as a stop with no place, and so no time in the schedule.

The coordinator handled it well. It told the user each time, gave its own September times, and saved a trip memory item to check again in spring 2027. But a real user sees a schedule that's wrong on two of six days, with warnings it says to ignore. The evaluations also score turns whose times are wrong.

The traces are in the `road-trip-agent` Phoenix project, on the `claude-code-sonnet` turns of 2026-11-05 from 01:29 to 01:46 UTC. The refusals are at 01:30:01, 01:30:12, 01:31:37, 01:45:36, and 01:45:39.

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 5 (out of scope: seasonal road and pass closures) and section 6.1 (checks).
- `src/google/routes-client.ts`, `requestFor`: the request sends no departure time, and is `TRAFFIC_UNAWARE`.

## Open questions

- Is this worth fixing, or is it a known limit of the out-of-scope line, to leave as it is?
- If it's worth fixing, which way? For example: find out whether a Google request option routes on the trip's date. Or let the agent set a stop's place and drive time by hand when Google finds no route. Or add a line to the coordinator's prompt so it plans around a closure that will be over, the way it did here.

## Do

- Find out whether Google Routes can route by a future date's road conditions, and say what it found.
- Then settle the open questions with Joe.

## Done when

- The open questions are settled, and the fix, if any, is in a PR.

## Ends in

A decision, or a PR.

**Settled in:** chat.
title: Routes use today's winter road closures for a trip months away

body:
## Why

This is the first general evaluator, and its main job is to teach the process of building one in Phoenix: writing a rubric, building a golden set with two strong models, tuning the rubric until a small judge model agrees with the golden set, and then scoring a whole corpus. A **general evaluator** checks how the coordinator does on any turn, not one behavior. This one asks a single question of each turn: is every fact in the coordinator's reply **grounded**, meaning it came from a source the coordinator had? It gives one verdict per turn, `grounded`, `not_grounded`, or `no_facts`, and lists the facts that weren't grounded. `no_facts` is for a reply with no facts to check, such as one that only asks questions, so those turns can be counted apart from the ones whose facts all check out. Added by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.

It scores only turns already recorded in Phoenix. Nothing is run again, and it doesn't lead to a prompt change. Whatever rate it finds is the result. The behavior evaluations (the issues labeled "Eval Canidate") are where turns get rerun with `npm run run-turn`, before and after a change.

Moved out of [Agent evaluations](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/issues/53), from the bullet "How are the evaluations built up?" in its open questions.

## Design

- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 5.
- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), section 10: the turns' traces in Phoenix.
- `src/agent/coordinator.view.md`: what the coordinator sees, including the two sentences the rubric copies (below).
- [research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.3 to 2.6: the #132 spike's judge on Haiku, and what it cost.

Terms used here:

- **The corpus:** the sessions in the `road-trip-agent` Phoenix project that have a session annotation named `corpus`, with identifier `corpus`. Its label is `real_user` or `simulated_user`, and its metadata names the trip, who played it, and the run's issue. On 2026-11-05 that's 21 sessions and 301 turns: 3 sessions Joe and his family played, and 18 from 9 simulated user runs. Sessions with a `not_for_evaluation` annotation are left out.
- **A turn:** one `coordinator.turn` span, with the spans under it in its trace.
- **Labelers:** two models that label sampled turns, each working alone, both on high effort: Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code, and GPT's Sol 6.1 in Codex. Opus 5.5 labeled the calibration sets in Sonnet's place. Neither sees the other's labels. The session that writes the rubric isn't a labeler.
- **Golden set:** the sampled turns with a settled label. That's either the label both labelers agree on, or Joe's call where he made one.
- **The judge:** Haiku 5.5, run with the rubric over the golden set, and then over the whole corpus.

## Open questions

- ~~How is `@arizeai/phoenix-client` installed for good? It names `@anthropic-ai/sdk` `^0.35.0` as an optional peer, and the app has 0.135.0, so `npm install` failed without `--legacy-peer-deps` in the #132 spike. The spike tested an `overrides` entry in `package.json` that fixed it with no flag (research/agent-evaluations.md, section 3). Check whether the current version still has the conflict. Moved from #53.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat: with an `overrides` entry. Checked the same day: 7.18.1 still names `^0.35.0`, which for a 0.x version allows only 0.35.x. Added to Do.
- ~~Later, should the allowed cases come from one shared piece of text? The coordinator's instructions and the rubric would both render it, so the rubric always matches the instructions at a given commit. That would remove the hand-copied sentences above. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat. Not needed for this corpus.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat: not for this project. The hand copy stays.
- ~~Should the rubric say a fair reading or summary of sourced facts is grounded? In the first set, on rubric `4343ba1`, Opus flagged a reply that listed a hotel's sourced 4.6-star rating, "the highest-rated of the three", under "Why it was offered", since the hotel's "Why" note doesn't name its rating. Joe called it too fine a point: a true reading of sourced facts. Sol didn't flag it. Held until the second set shows whether it comes up again. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat: no rubric change. It didn't come up in the second set, where both labelers took fair readings of sourced facts as grounded. Raise it again if it comes back.

## Do

**Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat:**

- **What counts as grounded.** A fact in a reply is grounded if it came from any of these:
  - a tool result, from this turn or an earlier turn in the session. This includes trip tool results, such as `read_itinerary`, since code works out much of what they say, such as schedule times, drive times with the buffer, and check results.
  - a worker's result, as the coordinator received it.
  - the user's own words.
  - the coordinator's own knowledge, but only where its instructions allow it, or as a general, guidebook-level description of a well-known place, such as "the Ferry Building is known for its food hall."

  Specific facts that can be checked always need a tool result: hours, prices, distances, drive times, addresses, whether a business exists, and current closures. The judge checks where a fact came from, not whether it's true. A made-up opening time fails even if it happens to be right.
- **Where the instructions allow the coordinator's own knowledge.** The rubric copies these two sentences from the coordinator's instructions, in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, rather than giving the judge the whole system prompt:
  - From the trip sketches step: "Sketches come from your own knowledge, not from research. … Seasonal closures and hazards also come from your own knowledge at this stage."
  - From the waypoints rule: "No tool shows the road a route takes, so judge that from your own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef."

  Trade-off: the rubric holds a copy. If the instructions change what the coordinator may say from its own knowledge, the judge keeps grading against the old rule until the rubric is updated by hand. Both sentences last changed on 2026-10-26, before the oldest corpus session (2026-10-30), so the copy holds for the whole corpus.
- **What the judge reads for a turn,** built by code from the turn's spans and the earlier turns in the same session:
  - each user message and reply in the session so far, including the date line.
  - each of the coordinator's tool results, labeled with the tool's name. For the 8 tools whose result doesn't say what it changed, the call's input too: `add_memory_item`, `update_memory_item`, `forget_memory_item`, `update_trip_brief`, `update_itinerary`, `update_day`, `update_stop`, and `update_stay`. Example: `add_memory_item` replies only "Added mem_x to this trip's memory.", so without the input the judge can't check "I've noted that you don't want to see the same thing twice." The input isn't a source for facts. It only shows what a successful change did. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set.
  - each worker shown only by its result, the `Agent` span's output. The worker's own searches are left out, since the coordinator never saw them.
  - the reply being judged.

  Left out: the system prompt, the other tools' inputs, and the coordinator's thinking. A tool call's input is the coordinator's own writing, so it isn't a source, and those tools' results already say what they did. Earlier sessions on the same trip are left out too, since the coordinator doesn't see them.
- **Every tool result counts as a source,** including text the coordinator wrote into the trip that a tool repeats back, such as a stop's purpose. Trade-off: a fact the coordinator made up, saved into the trip, and then repeated would pass. On 2026-11-05, every write to the trip in the live project since 2026-10-30 was checked, about 1,700 calls. The coordinator's writes held settings, such as a day's start time, the user's own words, and purposes. None held a made-up hour, price, or distance. The hours and distances in stop notes came from the workers' searches. If this starts to happen, code can mark the coordinator's own text in the results from the calls' inputs, so the judge doesn't have to tell them apart.
- **Only the coordinator is checked.** If a worker made a fact up, the coordinator passes for repeating it. Checking workers would be a separate evaluator.
- **TypeScript,** in `src/`, so `npm run check` covers it. It uses `@arizeai/phoenix-client` to read spans, write annotations, and run the experiments. The judge calls Haiku through the Anthropic SDK the app already has, with structured output in the labelers' JSON, and code works out the label the same way. Changed by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, from `phoenix-evals`' classifier, which can only return a label. Haiku through Claude Code on the 60 golden turns, listing every fact, matched 51 labels and found 92 of the 103 facts both labelers flagged. Listing only the ungrounded facts also matched 51, but found 87, and got more of Joe's close calls wrong.
- **The judge's prompt is a Phoenix prompt,** `grounded-judge`. The repo's `evals/grounded/rubric.md` stays the source. A command pushes each committed version to Phoenix, tagged with its commit, along with the model, `claude-haiku-5-5`, and high effort. The experiment fetches the prompt from Phoenix, so each experiment links to the prompt version it used. The judge uses `JUDGE_API_KEY` from `.env`. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.
- **Install `@arizeai/phoenix-client` with an `overrides` entry in `package.json`,** so it uses the app's `@anthropic-ai/sdk`. Its optional peer range, `^0.35.0`, doesn't fit the app's 0.135.0, and `npm install` fails without it. The other fix, `--legacy-peer-deps`, would have to be passed on every install, including the server's builds, and turns off the peer check for every package. The #132 spike tested the `overrides` entry (research/agent-evaluations.md, section 3). `phoenix-client` doesn't use the Anthropic SDK for anything this evaluator calls.
- **The labels are span annotations** on each turn's `coordinator.turn` span, all named `grounded`. Phoenix keeps one annotation per name and identifier on a span, so each labeler gets its own identifier, and writing again under the same identifier replaces only that one:
  - `sonnet-5.5` and `gpt-sol-6.1`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the labelers. The calibration sets also have `opus-5.5`, and the labelers tried there: `gpt-terra-6.1`, plus the medium-effort runs, with `-medium` on the end.
  - `joe`, annotator kind `HUMAN`, for Joe's calls.
  - `haiku-5.5`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the judge's corpus run. Its annotations are named `grounded-haiku`, not `grounded`. Phoenix's project page sums up annotations by name only, not by identifier, so under `grounded` the judge's rate would be mixed with the labelers' labels and Joe's calls on the 60 sampled turns. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.

  Each has the label `grounded`, `not_grounded`, or `no_facts`. `grounded` scores 1 and `not_grounded` scores 0. `no_facts` has no score, so Phoenix's average leaves those turns out, and the label still shows the turn was judged. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Each also has the ungrounded facts as its explanation, and the rubric's version in its metadata, with every fact the annotator listed. The version is the commit that last changed `evals/grounded/rubric.md`, such as `{"rubric": "abdae9d"}`, so `git show` gives the exact text. The labeling command refuses to run while the rubric has uncommitted changes. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. The first set's v1 labels say `v1`.
- **The golden set is a Phoenix dataset,** `grounded-golden`. Each example holds a turn's judge input and span ID, and its settled label. For the 15 turns Joe called, it also holds his ungrounded facts. Its metadata holds the set, where the label came from, and both labelers' ungrounded facts. Sol's list isn't treated as the truth, since Joe's calls on the 5 label splits all went against it. When Joe changes a call, the golden set command updates only the changed turns, as a new version of the dataset. Replacing the dataset would delete the experiments run on it. Each experiment is scored against the labels at the time it ran, so comparing versions across a label change means scoring them again against the current labels.
- **Each rubric version is a Phoenix experiment.** The judge runs with that version over the golden set, and a code check marks whether its label matches the settled one. Phoenix keeps each experiment, so versions can be compared turn by turn. Each experiment judges every turn 3 times, since a run's score moves by about 2 turns from one run to the next. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-07, in chat. The experiment's description is the rubric commit's subject line, so that subject says what the version changed. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.

**The steps, in order:**

1. **Pick the sample.** Code picks about 60 turns from the corpus, about one in five, with at least one from every session, and the same turns for both labelers. The pick is repeatable, such as from a fixed seed, and it's done in sets of 5.
2. **Build each sampled turn's judge input** as its own file, ending with that turn's reply, so a labeler can't see anything that came later in the session.
3. **Draft rubric v1** from the decisions above. Joe reviews its wording.
4. **Label a set of 5.** Opus and Sol each label the set alone, and return JSON listing every fact in each turn's reply, with its source and whether it's grounded. Code works out the label from the list: no facts is `no_facts`, any ungrounded fact is `not_grounded`, and otherwise `grounded`. With only the ungrounded facts, there's no telling whether a labeler checked a fact and passed it, or never saw it. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set. Code checks the JSON and writes the annotations. Each labeler runs from a folder outside the repo, as the simulated users do (`simulated-users/README.md`, "Start a harness"), so it doesn't load the repo's `CLAUDE.md` or Joe's own. Run Sol on high effort, which Codex shows as `GPT-6.1-Sol high`. Codex starts it on a lower effort by default, and Joe has had better results on high. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Opus and Sol labeled the calibration sets.
5. **Joe reviews the set.** A review page shows each turn's judge input in a form that's easy for a person to read, since the raw spans in Phoenix are hard to follow. The page shows only the judge input, not the labels. The agent gives both labelers' labels and flagged facts in chat. For the first sets, Joe reviews every turn, agreements included, and looks into each one in chat with the agent's help. He tells the agent his call in chat, and the agent saves it as the `joe` annotation with a command. The review page only reads. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat, and changed on 2026-11-06 to leave the labels off the page.
6. **Refine the rubric,** and repeat steps 4 and 5 with a new set of 5, until Joe says the rubric is good. The hope is two sets.
7. **Label the rest of the 60** with Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1, both on high effort. On the two calibration sets, Sonnet matched Joe as well as Opus did, for less, and a rerun gave the same labels. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat; the comparison is in a comment. The agent tells Joe in chat which turns the labelers disagree on, and Joe reviews only those, the same way.
8. **Build the golden set,** and run the judge on it as an experiment, one for each rubric version. Tune the rubric until Joe says the judge agrees well enough.
9. **Run the judge over the whole corpus,** writing the `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`. Report the rate, such as 12 of 301 turns not grounded, with what the ungrounded facts were like, in a comment on this issue.
10. **Write how the evaluator runs** into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.

## Done when

- The `grounded` annotations from both labelers, and Joe's calls, are on the sampled turns.
- The golden set is a dataset in Phoenix, with an experiment for each rubric version tried.
- The judge's `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`, from the final rubric version, are on all corpus turns, and the rate is reported in a comment here.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR, with the code, the rubric, and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5. The run's results go in a comment on this issue.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

nodes.body:
## Labeler comparison on the two calibration sets

All runs used rubric `34276ea`, on the 10 turns in sets 1 and 2. Joe's calls on those turns list 8 ungrounded facts, across 5 `not_grounded` turns.

| Labeler | Labels matching Joe (of 10) | Joe's 8 facts found | Facts flagged that Joe didn't |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5, high | 10 | 7 | 0 |
| Sol 6.1, high | 10 | 8 | 0 |
| Sonnet 5.5, high | 10 | 7 | 1 |
| Sonnet 5.5, medium | 10 | 7 | 5 |
| Sol 6.1, medium | 9 | 7 | 4 |
| Terra 6.1, high | 8 | 8 | 13 |
| Terra 6.1, medium | 9 | 8 | 10 |

- Opus and Sonnet both missed "I kept the Mel Fisher Maritime Museum there" (set 1, turn `0f5c6607a087c647`). The Key West stop never had a place selected. Sonnet's extra flag was "typical with the guided tour" for the Hemingway Home, which Joe called a judgment call.
- Terra, on either effort, and Sol on medium flagged fair readings, such as "I've set the trip up as 5 days" when the trip brief said 5 and the itinerary still had 1 day. That turned grounded turns into `not_grounded`.
- A second run of Sonnet and Sol on high gave the same 10 labels. Sol flagged exactly Joe's 8 facts again. Sonnet found the same 7, and its guided tour flag didn't come back.

Joe chose Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1, both on high, for the remaining 50 turns.

**Corpus run results (step 9)**

The judge, Haiku 5.5 on rubric v7 (`b66b866`), called **221 of the 301 corpus turns not grounded (73%)**, and 80 grounded. Every turn got an answer. The labels are on the turns' spans as `grounded-haiku` annotations, identifier `haiku-5.5`.

**How far to trust the rate.** On the golden set, v7 matched the settled label in 167 of 180 runs (93%, 3 runs per turn). It flagged 8 grounded turns and missed 2 ungrounded ones, so it leans a little strict. The golden labels put 42 of 60 sampled turns at not grounded (70%), so the true corpus rate is likely about 70%. The rubric was tuned on those same 60 turns, so 93% is somewhat optimistic for turns the judge hasn't seen.

**Rubric versions tried**, scored on today's golden labels:

| Rubric | What changed | Matched (of 180) |
|---|---|---|
| v3 `34276ea` | Baseline | 156 |
| v4 `db82cec` | Times the coordinator estimates are plans. Replaced by v5. | 148 |
| v5 `aa2590f` | A time it picks is a plan. A worked-out arrival time needs the times it's worked out from. | 159 |
| v6 `04007ef` | Its judgment of the plan is an opinion. Claims about what the checks found need check results. | 166 |
| v7 `b66b866` | A claim that goes past what the checks show still needs a source. | 167 |

Joe changed two golden labels during tuning, both to grounded, since the times could be worked out from the record: the Hungry Horse arrival (set 5) and the Salt Lake City arrival (set 12).

**What the ungrounded facts are like.** The judge flagged 774 of the 4,376 facts it listed, usually about 3 in a flagged turn, at most 16. Sorted roughly by keywords:
- Drive times, walk times, and distances: about 30%, such as "are a short drive apart" for the Newport mansions.
- Opening hours and closures: about 20%.
- Times of day and schedules: about 17%, such as "SpaceX launches out of the Cape often, sometimes several times a week".
- Descriptions of a business beyond what the sources say: about 7%, such as "It's famous for its themed rooms" for the Madonna Inn.
- Reservations and prices: about 5%. Claims of changing the trip: under 1%. The rest is mixed.

The grounded share per session runs from 0 to 0.67.

**Cost.** About $0.007 a turn on the API. The November 7 experiments, 720 judge calls, cost $5.13.

title: General evaluator: grounded in the record

body:
## Why

Trip memory holds notes the trip brief and the itinerary can't, such as a soft intention ("wants one nice dinner in Austin") or an open item (functional spec 10.2). As the plan fills in, some of those notes get done, and then they repeat what the itinerary holds. The coordinator should update or forget them then. When it doesn't, a new session reads a note that looks like open work but is already planned, or one that disagrees with the itinerary.

#209 grades only whether each save goes to the right place. Keeping memory up to date as the plan changes is a different behavior, so it was left out there (decided by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat). This issue is for an evaluation of it, if it's ever worth doing. Joe expects to move on to another project after #209, so it may never be picked up.

## The cases

Found while reading the saving corpus for #209, set 1 (`evals/saving/turns.json`). Each span is a `coordinator.turn` span in the `road-trip-agent` project in Phoenix.

- **The Bar Harbor trip,** span `e8ff5e9c4d6022a6` (turn 3). Trip memory item mem_3cntqap8 holds "Julia wants one nice dinner in Portland. The trip needs at least one night there", among other notes. Once that dinner is planned, the note should be forgotten.
- **The Albuquerque trip,** span `0c2867c2dbd0a68e` (turn 3). Trip memory item mem_t8m6zzmt says where the trip ends. It's fine while the itinerary doesn't show it. Once the itinerary does, the item repeats it and should be forgotten.

## Open questions

- Is this worth an evaluation at all? Proposal: only if #209's results show stale memory misleading a later session.
- What does it check? Proposal: after each turn that changes the itinerary, no trip memory item repeats what the itinerary now holds, unless it adds a reason or a hard limit (the dates rule in #209's decision log, `evals/saving/decisions.md`).

## Do

- Nothing until the open questions are settled.

## Done when

- The open questions are settled, or the issue is closed as not needed.

## Ends in

A decision.

**Settled in:** chat.
title: Evaluate whether the coordinator keeps trip memory up to date as the plan fills in

body:
## Why

Claude Code saves the request it builds for a session, the system prompt with the tools, as a `prompt_snapshot` line in the session's transcript. A resumed session sends that saved copy again, instead of the `systemPrompt` and tools the app passes in. Every turn after a session's first resumes it (`src/agent/coordinator.ts`, `coordinatorOptions`). So a session keeps the coordinator's instructions and tools from its first turn, and a deployed change to them reaches only sessions started after it.

That makes agent behavior hard to trace. A turn's trace names the commit the app ran (`metadata.commit`), but the model ran on the instructions of whatever commit started the session. A behavior change after a deploy may be missing from trips already under way, with nothing in the trace that says why.

Found in #209: the saving replays resume recorded sessions, and every replay ran on the instructions the session was recorded with. The first input of each turn had the same token count before and after a 5,700-character change to the instructions. `src/turn-run/recorded-turn.ts` now leaves the snapshots out of a run's copy of the transcript. A run of case 4.10 then wrote a new snapshot with the new instructions.

## Open questions

1. Should a live session pick up the instructions and tools of the code that runs each turn? One way is what `recorded-turn.ts` does: leave the snapshot lines out when the transcript is loaded for a resume, and give the line after each one the snapshot's parent. A session's prompt cache would be rebuilt after each deploy that changes them. The other is to keep it as it is, and say in technical spec 5.2 that a session keeps its first turn's instructions.

## Do

- Confirm it in the app: change the coordinator's instructions locally, resume a session started before the change with `npm run chat`, and check its transcript for a new `prompt_snapshot`, and the first model call's input tokens in the trace.

## Done when

- Open question 1 is settled, and the app does what it says.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR, or a decision written in technical spec 5.2.

## Settled in

Chat.
title: A resumed session keeps the instructions and tools of its first turn
